However, the longer argument reveals more of the structure: the residual degrees of freedom arise from the orthogonal decomposition of the random response into fitted and residual components. We can now choose the constant \(a\) in \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = a \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}}. \] Proposition 7.11 (Unbiased Estimator of the Error Variance) Consider estimators of the form \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = a \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \] where \(a\) is a constant scalar. Under the mean and variance assumptions, \[ \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\sigma}^2 ight] = \sigma^2 \] if and only if \[  oxed{ a =  rac{1}{ n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) }. } \] Therefore, \[  oxed{ \hat{\sigma}^2 =  rac{ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} }{ n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) } } \] is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\). For a full-column-rank model with an intercept and \(p\) explanatory variables, \[  oxed{ \hat{\sigma}^2 =  rac{ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} }{ n-p-1 }. } \] Proof Proof. Since \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = a \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \] we have \[  egin{aligned} \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\sigma}^2 ight] &= \mathbb{E} \left[ a \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} ight] \ &= a \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} ight] && 	ext{lin. exp.} \ &= a \sigma^2 \left( n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) ight) && 	ext{expected RSS}. \end{aligned} \] Therefore, \[  egin{aligned} \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\sigma}^2 ight] = \sigma^2 &\iff a \sigma^2 \left( n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) ight) = \sigma^2 \ &\iff a \left( n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) ight) = 1 \ &\iff  oxed{ a =  rac{1}{ n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) }. } \end{aligned} \] Thus, among estimators of the form \[ a \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \] with \(a\) a constant scalar, unbiasedness uniquely determines the value of \(a\). This does not imply that \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) is the only possible unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\). The uniqueness statement applies only within this particular class of estimators. At this stage, we have established \[  oxed{ \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\sigma}^2 ight] = \sigma^2. } \] This conclusion uses only the mean and variance assumptions. We still do not know the probability distribution of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). The next chapter will introduce the Normality assumption, \[ \mathbf{e} \sim N \left( \mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I} ight). \] Under Normality, the residual sum of squares will satisfy \[  oxed{  rac{ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} }{ \sigma^2 } \sim \chi^2_{ n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) }. } \] Thus, the progression is \[  oxed{  egin{array}{c} 	ext{Mean and variance assumptions} \ \Downarrow \ 	ext{unbiased estimation of }\sigma^2 \[3mm] 	ext{Normality assumption} \ \Downarrow \ 	ext{sampling distribution of }\hat{\sigma}^2. \end{array} } \] This completes the development of the first two moments of the linear regression model and prepares the way for exact distributional inference. 7.6 Synthesis This chapter marks an important change in the interpretation of the linear regression model. In the previous chapters, the model \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta} + \mathbf{e} \] was studied primarily through optimization and linear algebra. Given an observed response vector \(\mathbf{y}\) and design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\), least squares produced \[ \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}, \] together with the fitted values \[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y} \] and residuals \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}. \] No probabilistic assumptions were needed to obtain these quantities or to establish their geometric properties. In this chapter, the algebraic form of the model remained unchanged, but its interpretation changed. The response became a random vector generated according to \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta} + \mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) is treated as fixed, \( oldsymbol{ eta}\) is an unknown parameter vector, and \(\mathbf{e}\) represents the random contribution not explicitly represented by the observed explanatory variables. The first two probabilistic assumptions then determined the first two moments of this model. The mean assumption, \[  oxed{ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}] = \mathbf{0}, } \] is equivalent to \[  oxed{ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] = \mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta}. } \] Thus, zero-mean errors and the interpretation of \(\mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta}\) as the mean response are two equivalent descriptions of the same mean structure. This assumption also gives the least-squares estimator an important statistical property: \[  oxed{ \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] =  oldsymbol{ eta}. } \] The quantity that was originally obtained as the solution to an optimization problem is therefore also an unbiased estimator of the parameter vector. Similarly, the variance assumption, \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{e}] = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}, } \] is equivalent to \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{y}] = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}. } \] Under the fixed-design formulation, the response and error vectors differ only by the fixed vector \(\mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta}\), so they have exactly the same covariance matrix. Together, the two assumptions give \[  oxed{ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] = \mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta}, \qquad \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{y}] = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}. } \] These equations specify the first two moments of the response, but they do not specify its complete distribution. The variance assumption also reveals an important connection between the probabilistic model and the geometry developed previously. The covariance matrices of the principal least-squares quantities are \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V} \left[ \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}, } \] \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} ight] = \sigma^2\mathbf{H}, } \] and \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} ight] = \sigma^2(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}). } \] The matrices \(\mathbf{H}\) and \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}\) are the same complementary projection matrices that appeared in the deterministic analysis of least squares. Previously, they determined where the fitted values and residuals lie geometrically. Now they also determine how those random quantities vary. This connection is particularly clear at the observation level: \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{y}_i] = \sigma^2h_{ii}, \] while \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{e}_i] = \sigma^2(1-h_{ii}). \] Therefore, \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V}[\hat{y}_i] + \mathbb{V}[\hat{e}_i] = \sigma^2 = \mathbb{V}[y_i]. } \] Leverage, which originally arose from the geometry of projection, now also controls how the variability of the response is divided between its fitted and residual components. The same progression appears in the cross-covariance results. From the deterministic geometry of least squares, \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{y}} = 0. \] Under the variance assumption, we additionally obtain \[ \mathbb{C} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \hat{\mathbf{y}} ight] = \mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{C} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] = \mathbf{0}. \] These results should not be confused. The first is a deterministic statement about geometric orthogonality for every fitted dataset. The latter are probabilistic statements about cross-covariances across repeated realizations of the random response. Thus, one of the central patterns of the chapter is \[  oxed{ 	ext{linear algebra} \quad\longrightarrow\quad 	ext{projection geometry} \quad\longrightarrow\quad 	ext{probabilistic consequences}. } \] The Gauss–Markov result provides another important connection between the deterministic and probabilistic viewpoints. Least squares was derived without probabilistic assumptions. However, once we impose \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}] = \mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{e}] = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}, \] we can establish that OLS is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator. For every linear unbiased estimator \(	ilde{ oldsymbol{ eta}}\), \[  oxed{ \mathbb{V} \left[ 	ilde{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] - \mathbb{V} \left[ \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] \succeq \mathbf{0}. } \] Thus, the assumptions are not needed to construct the OLS estimator. They are needed to establish its statistical properties and optimality. The distinction is \[  oxed{ 	ext{optimization} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}}, } \] followed by \[  oxed{ 	ext{mean and variance assumptions} \quad\longrightarrow\quad 	ext{unbiasedness and Gauss--Markov optimality}. } \] The MSE results reinforce this interpretation. For any vector estimator, \[ \operatorname{MSE} \left( 	ilde{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight) = \operatorname{tr} \left( \mathbb{V} \left[ 	ilde{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] ight) + \left\| \operatorname{Bias} \left( 	ilde{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight) ight\|^2. \] Among linear unbiased estimators, the bias term vanishes, so the Gauss–Markov covariance ordering also implies that OLS minimizes this scalar MSE criterion. Finally, the chapter introduced the unknown variance parameter \(\sigma^2\) and showed how it can be estimated using the residuals. The key result is \[ \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} ight] = \sigma^2 \left( n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) ight). \] This leads to the unbiased estimator \[  oxed{ \hat{\sigma}^2 =  rac{ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} }{ n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) }. } \] For a full-column-rank model containing an intercept and \(p\) explanatory variables, \[  oxed{ \hat{\sigma}^2 =  rac{ \hat{\mathbf{e}}' \hat{\mathbf{e}} }{ n-p-1 }. } \] The denominator has a geometric meaning. Since \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}, \] the residual vector lies in \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp, \] whose dimension is \[ n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}). \] The residual degrees of freedom therefore arise directly from the dimension of the residual subspace. At the end of this chapter, we know a substantial amount about the regression model using only assumptions about its first two moments. We have obtained unbiasedness, covariance matrices, zero cross-covariances, Gauss–Markov optimality, and an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\). What we still do not know are the complete probability distributions of these quantities. In particular, \[ \mathbb{C} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \hat{ oldsymbol{ eta}} ight] = \mathbf{0} \] does not yet imply independence, and \[ \mathbb{E} \left[ \hat{\sigma}^2 ight] = \sigma^2 \] does not determine the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). These limitations explain why the next assumption is needed. The Normality assumption will not be introduced to derive OLS or to establish that it is BLUE. Those results are already available. Instead, Normality will convert the moment results developed here into exact distributional results: \[  oxed{  egin{array}{c} 	ext{Mean and variance assumptions} \ \Downarrow \ 	ext{expectations, covariances, unbiasedness, and optimality} \[3mm] 	ext{Normality assumption} \ \Downarrow \ 	ext{independence and exact sampling distributions} \ \Downarrow \ 	ext{confidence intervals and hypothesis tests}. \end{array} } \] The algebra and geometry of least squares therefore remain unchanged throughout this progression. What changes is the amount of probabilistic structure imposed on the data-generating mechanism and, consequently, the strength of the statistical conclusions that can be drawn. 7.7 Exercises Consider the regression model \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} oldsymbol{ eta} + \mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) is fixed and has full column rank. 8 Normality Assumption 8.1 Introduction In the previous chapter, we introduced a probabilistic interpretation of the linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}. \] The design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) was treated as fixed, the coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) as an unknown parameter, and the error vector \(\mathbf{e}\) as random. We then imposed assumptions on the first two moments of the errors, \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}]=\mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{e}]=\sigma^2\mathbf{I}. \] These assumptions were sufficient to establish many important statistical properties of the least squares estimators. In particular, we obtained \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \boldsymbol{\beta} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}, \] as well as the corresponding expectations and covariance matrices of the fitted values and residuals. We also studied their cross-covariances, established the Gauss–Markov result, and constructed an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\) from the residual sum of squares. None of these results required us to specify the complete probability distribution of the errors. They depended only on assumptions about their mean, variance, and covariance structure. There are, however, statistical questions that cannot be answered from these moments alone. For example, suppose that we want to determine how likely it is for an estimated coefficient to differ substantially from its true value. We may want to construct an interval that contains an unknown coefficient with a prescribed probability, determine whether an observed estimate is unusually far from a hypothesized value, or determine how likely a hypothesis test is to detect a particular alternative. Questions of this type require the sampling distributions of the estimators and test statistics, rather than only their expectations and variances. We will therefore strengthen the assumptions on the error vector. Throughout this chapter, we assume \[ \boxed{ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). } \] This assumption contains the mean and variance assumptions from the previous chapter, \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}]=\mathbf{0}, \qquad \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{e}]=\sigma^2\mathbf{I}, \] but provides considerably more information by specifying the complete distribution of \(\mathbf{e}\). It is important to distinguish what changes when this assumption is introduced from what does not. The least squares estimator remains \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}. \] Normality is not required to derive this estimator. It is also not required for its unbiasedness or for the Gauss–Markov result. Those properties were established previously under weaker assumptions. What Normality gives us is additional information about the stochastic behavior of the quantities that we have already constructed. Since \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e} \] and \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is non-random, \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}) \] is equivalent to \[ \mathbf{y} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Many of the quantities developed previously are linear transformations of \(\mathbf{y}\). For example, \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}, \] \[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}, \] and \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}. \] Because linear transformations of multivariate Normal random vectors remain multivariate Normal, the expectations and covariance matrices obtained in the previous chapter can now be used to determine the complete distributions of these quantities. Normality also strengthens some of the relationships that we previously obtained from covariance calculations. For example, we showed that \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\mathbf{y}}] = \mathbf{0}. \] Without an additional distributional assumption, zero cross-covariance does not generally imply independence. Under joint Normality, however, it does. This distinction will be essential when we combine the distribution of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) with the independent estimator \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) to obtain Student’s \(t\) and \(F\) distributions. The first part of this chapter will therefore use Normality to derive the exact sampling distributions of \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{e}}, \qquad \hat{\sigma}^2. \] These distributions provide the basis for interval estimation. We will construct confidence intervals for regression coefficients and general linear combinations of coefficients, intervals for the expected response, prediction intervals for future observations, and an interval estimator for \(\sigma^2\). The same sampling distributions will then be used for hypothesis testing. We will study tests for individual coefficients, the overall regression, and groups of coefficients. In particular, the geometric structure developed in previous chapters will reappear through comparisons of nested regression models and the corresponding reductions in residual variation. Hypothesis testing studies the behavior of a statistic under a null hypothesis. We will then extend this perspective through power analysis by studying the distribution of the same statistics when the null hypothesis is false. This will introduce noncentral \(t\) and \(F\) distributions and show how the ability to detect an effect depends on its magnitude, the error variability, and the information contained in the regression design. Thus, Normality allows us to study not only whether a test controls its probability of rejection under a null hypothesis, but also how effectively it can distinguish that null hypothesis from particular alternatives. Finally, specifying the complete distribution of \(\mathbf{y}\) has another consequence that is conceptually distinct from the inferential developments above. Since \[ \mathbf{y} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}), \] we can construct a likelihood function for the unknown parameters and estimate them using Maximum Likelihood Estimation. This provides a second route to estimation. Under the Normal linear regression model, Maximum Likelihood Estimation produces the same estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) as least squares, \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{MLE} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{OLS}, \] but it produces a different estimator of \(\sigma^2\) from the unbiased estimator used in classical regression inference. This distinction will illustrate that least squares, unbiased estimation, and maximum likelihood are different estimation principles, even when some of them lead to the same estimator. The role of the Normality assumption in this chapter can therefore be summarized through three related consequences: \[ \boxed{ \begin{array}{c} \text{Normality} \\[4pt] \Downarrow \\[4pt] \text{Exact sampling distributions} \\[4pt] \Downarrow \\[4pt] \text{Interval estimation, hypothesis testing, and power} \end{array} } \] and, separately, \[ \boxed{ \begin{array}{c} \text{Normal probability model} \\[4pt] \Downarrow \\[4pt] \text{Likelihood function} \\[4pt] \Downarrow \\[4pt] \text{Maximum Likelihood Estimation}. \end{array} } \] The first sequence develops the inferential consequences of Normality. The second uses the same distributional assumption as an alternative principle for estimation. Together, they show why specifying the complete distribution of the errors substantially expands what can be learned from the linear regression model. 8.2 Distribution of the Estimates In the previous chapter, we derived the expectations and covariance matrices of the least squares estimators using only assumptions on the first two moments of the errors. In particular, we did not need to specify the complete distribution of the error vector. We now add the Normality assumption \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Since \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is non-random, it follows immediately that \[ \mathbf{y}\sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] The Normality assumption now allows us to go beyond the expectations and covariance matrices derived previously. Since a linear transformation of a multivariate Normal random vector is also multivariate Normal, any quantity that is a linear transformation of \(\mathbf{y}\) will have a Normal distribution whose mean and covariance matrix are already available from the previous chapter. 8.2.1 Distribution of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), and \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) The quantities \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}, \] \[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}, \] and \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y} \] are all linear transformations of \(\mathbf{y}\). Their complete distributions therefore follow directly from Normality together with the expectations and covariance matrices derived previously. Proposition 8.1 (Distribution of the Linear Least Squares Quantities) Under the linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}), \] the least squares estimator, fitted values, and residuals satisfy \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right), \] \[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{H} \right), \] and \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{0}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) \right). \] Proof Proof. Since \[ \mathbf{y}\sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}), \] and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is a linear transformation of \(\mathbf{y}\), we know that \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is multivariate Normal. From the previous chapter, \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \boldsymbol{\beta} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}. \] Therefore, \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right). \] Similarly, \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}\) is a linear transformation of \(\mathbf{y}\). From the previous chapter, \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathbf{y}}] = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\mathbf{y}}] = \sigma^2\mathbf{H}. \] Therefore, \[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{H} \right). \] Finally, \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}\) is also a linear transformation of \(\mathbf{y}\). We previously showed that \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathbf{e}}] = \mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\mathbf{e}}] = \sigma^2(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}). \] Therefore, \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{0}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) \right). \] The Normality assumption has therefore converted the moment results from the previous chapter into complete distributional results. For example, \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \boldsymbol{\beta} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \] were already known. Normality now allows us to conclude the stronger result \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right). \] The covariance matrices of \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) are singular. This is expected from their geometric interpretation. The fitted values are restricted to the column space of \(\mathbf{X}\), while the residuals are restricted to its orthogonal complement. Thus, their distributions are multivariate Normal distributions supported on lower-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The estimator \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) is different. Recall that \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1}, \] where \(p\) is the number of explanatory variables and the model contains an intercept. Unlike the previous quantities, \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) is not a linear transformation of \(\mathbf{y}\). Instead, it depends on the quadratic form \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}\). Its distribution therefore requires a different argument. 8.2.2 Distribution of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) We begin by expressing the residual sum of squares in terms of the random error vector. Since \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}, \] we have \[\begin{align*} \hat{\mathbf{e}} &= (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}) && \text{since $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}$} \\ &= (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e}\\ &= \mathbf{0}+(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e} && \text{since $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}$} \\ &= (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e}. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[\begin{align*} \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}} &= \mathbf{e}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e}\\ &= \mathbf{e}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e} && \text{since $(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})$ is symmetric} \\ &= \mathbf{e}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e} && \text{since $(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})$ is idempotent}. \end{align*}\] Now define \[ \mathbf{z} = \frac{\mathbf{e}}{\sigma}. \] Since \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}), \] we have \[ \mathbf{z}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). \] Thus, \[\begin{align*} \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} &= \frac{\mathbf{e}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{e}}{\sigma^2} \\ &= \left(\frac{\mathbf{e}}{\sigma}\right)' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) \left(\frac{\mathbf{e}}{\sigma}\right) \\ &= \mathbf{z}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{z}. \end{align*}\] The distribution of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) therefore reduces to determining the distribution of a quadratic form involving a standard multivariate Normal vector and a symmetric idempotent matrix. Proposition 8.2 (Normal Quadratic Form with a Symmetric Idempotent Matrix) Let \[ \mathbf{z}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) \] with \(\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be a symmetric idempotent matrix of rank \(m\). Then \[ \mathbf{z}'\mathbf{M}\mathbf{z} \sim \chi^2_m. \] Proof Proof. Since \(\mathbf{M}\) is symmetric, it has the spectral decomposition \[ \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}', \] where \(\mathbf{V}\) is an orthogonal matrix and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{M}\). Since \(\mathbf{M}\) is idempotent, \[ \mathbf{M}^2=\mathbf{M}. \] Therefore, if \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{M}\), then \[ \lambda^2=\lambda, \] which implies \[ \lambda\in\{0,1\}. \] Since \[ \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{M})=m, \] exactly \(m\) eigenvalues are equal to \(1\), while the remaining \(n-m\) eigenvalues are equal to \(0\). Without loss of generality, we can write \[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \operatorname{diag} ( \underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{m}, \underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{n-m} ). \] Now define \[ \mathbf{w}=\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{z}. \] Since \(\mathbf{w}\) is a linear transformation of the multivariate Normal vector \(\mathbf{z}\), it is also multivariate Normal. Its mean is \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{w}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{z}] = \mathbf{V}'\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}] = \mathbf{0}, \] and its covariance matrix is \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{w}] &= \mathbf{V}'\mathbb{V}[\mathbf{z}]\mathbf{V}\\ &= \mathbf{V}'\mathbf{I}\mathbf{V}\\ &= \mathbf{V}'\mathbf{V}\\ &= \mathbf{I}. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[ \mathbf{w}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). \] In particular, the components \[ w_1,\ldots,w_n \] are independent standard Normal random variables. We can now rewrite the quadratic form as \[\begin{align*} \mathbf{z}'\mathbf{M}\mathbf{z} &= \mathbf{z}'(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}')\mathbf{z} && \text{using the spectral decomposition of $\mathbf{M}$} \\ &= (\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{z})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{z}) \\ &= \mathbf{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w} && \text{since $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{z}$} \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^n[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}]_{ii}w_i^2 \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^m w_i^2 && \text{since exactly $m$ diagonal entries of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ are equal to $1$}. \end{align*}\] Since \(w_1,\ldots,w_m\) are independent standard Normal random variables, \[ \sum_{i=1}^m w_i^2 \sim \chi^2_m \] by the definition of the chi-squared distribution. Therefore, \[ \mathbf{z}'\mathbf{M}\mathbf{z} \sim \chi^2_m. \] This proposition connects the geometry of projection matrices with the chi-squared distribution. A symmetric idempotent matrix retains the components of \(\mathbf{z}\) lying in a particular subspace. Its rank determines the dimension of that subspace and, consequently, the number of independent squared standard Normal components appearing in the quadratic form. We can now apply this result to the residual sum of squares. Proposition 8.3 (Distribution of the Residual Variance Estimator) Consider the linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, the model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Then, \[ \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] Equivalently, \[ \frac{(n-p-1)\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}, \] and therefore \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \sim \frac{\sigma^2}{n-p-1} \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] Proof Proof. We have already shown that \[ \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} = \mathbf{z}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{z}, \] where \[ \mathbf{z}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). \] The matrix \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric and idempotent. Furthermore, \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) &= n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H}) \\ &= n-\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}) \\ &= n-(p+1) \\ &= n-p-1. \end{align*}\] Therefore, by Proposition 8.2, \[ \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] Since \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1}, \] we have \[\begin{align*} \frac{(n-p-1)\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} &= \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} \\ &\sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \end{align*}\] Equivalently, \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \sim \frac{\sigma^2}{n-p-1}\chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] The appearance of \(n-p-1\) is not arbitrary. Recall that \[ \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})=n-p-1. \] Thus, the residual degrees of freedom are exactly the dimension of the residual subspace. The chi-squared distribution arises because, under Normality, the residual sum of squares can be represented as the sum of squares of \(n-p-1\) independent standard Normal components. This result gives considerably more information than the result obtained in the previous chapter. There we showed only that \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}^2]=\sigma^2. \] Normality now determines the complete distribution of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). 8.2.3 Independence of the Least Squares Components The previous chapter also established that the residuals are uncorrelated with both the fitted values and the estimated coefficients: \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\mathbf{y}}] = \mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \mathbf{0}. \] Without further assumptions, these results do not imply independence. Two random quantities can be uncorrelated and still be dependent. Normality changes this conclusion. Since \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) are all linear transformations of the Normal vector \(\mathbf{y}\), the corresponding pairs are jointly Normal. For jointly Normal random vectors, zero cross-covariance implies independence. Proposition 8.4 (Independence of Residuals from Fitted Values and Coefficient Estimates) Under the Normal linear regression model, \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \perp \hat{\mathbf{y}} \] and \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \perp \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] Consequently, \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \perp \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] Proof Proof. Since \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) are both linear transformations of the multivariate Normal vector \(\mathbf{y}\), they are jointly multivariate Normal. From the previous chapter, \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\mathbf{y}}] = \mathbf{0}. \] Therefore, joint Normality and zero cross-covariance imply \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \perp \hat{\mathbf{y}}. \] Similarly, \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) are jointly Normal because both are linear transformations of \(\mathbf{y}\). We previously showed that \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \mathbf{0}. \] Therefore, \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \perp \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] Finally, \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1} \] is a function only of \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\). Since \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) are independent, any function of \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\) is also independent of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\). Hence, \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \perp \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] This last result will be particularly important for inference. We now have two distinct pieces of information about the coefficient estimator: \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right) \] and \[ \frac{(n-p-1)\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}, \] with \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \perp \hat{\sigma}^2. \] The first result describes the variation in the estimated coefficients when \(\sigma^2\) is known. The second provides a random estimate of the unknown \(\sigma^2\). Their independence will allow these two results to be combined to obtain Student’s \(t\) distributions, which will provide the basis for interval estimation and hypothesis testing in the following sections. 8.3 Interval Estimation In the previous section, we obtained the sampling distributions of the least squares estimators. These distributions describe how the estimators would vary across repeated realizations of the regression model. A point estimator provides a single estimate of an unknown parameter. For example, \[ \hat{\beta}_j \] provides a point estimate of \(\beta_j\). However, the fact that an estimator is random means that different realizations of the response vector generally produce different estimates. A point estimate by itself does not describe this uncertainty. The sampling distributions derived previously allow us to construct interval estimators. Before the data are observed, the endpoints of an interval estimator are random. We will construct these intervals so that they contain the unknown quantity of interest with a specified probability. After the data are observed, the resulting interval is fixed. At that point, the unknown parameter either belongs to the interval or it does not. The confidence level describes the proportion of intervals constructed in this way that would contain the true parameter under repeated realizations of the model. We begin by establishing notation for the distributional quantiles that will be used throughout interval estimation and hypothesis testing. 8.3.1 Quantile Notation Definition 8.1 (Upper-Tail Distribution Quantiles) For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), we use upper-tail quantiles defined by \[ \mathbb{P}(Z\geq z_\alpha)=\alpha, \qquad Z\sim N(0,1), \] \[ \mathbb{P}(T\geq t_{\nu,\alpha})=\alpha, \qquad T\sim t_\nu, \] \[ \mathbb{P}(W\geq \chi^2_{\nu,\alpha})=\alpha, \qquad W\sim\chi^2_\nu, \] and \[ \mathbb{P}(F\geq f_{q,\nu,\alpha})=\alpha, \qquad F\sim F_{q,\nu}. \] These quantiles are fixed values determined by the corresponding distribution, its degrees of freedom when applicable, and the upper-tail probability \(\alpha\). For example, since the \(t\) distribution is symmetric, \[ \mathbb{P} \left( -t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \leq T \leq t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \right) = 1-\alpha. \] Thus, throughout the chapter, \(\alpha\) will denote the total probability outside a two-sided confidence interval, while \(1-\alpha\) will denote its confidence level. 8.3.2 Linear Combinations of the Regression Coefficients Many quantities of interest in linear regression can be expressed as linear combinations of the regression coefficients. Suppose that the model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, so that \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}. \] For a fixed nonzero vector \[ \mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}, \] consider the quantity \[ \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}. \] Different choices of \(\mathbf{a}\) will allow us to study an individual coefficient, the expected response at a new predictor vector, or other linear combinations of the regression coefficients. From the distribution derived previously, \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right). \] Therefore, \[ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} \right). \] If \(\sigma^2\) were known, we could immediately standardize this quantity using its true standard deviation. However, \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. The previous section showed that it can be estimated independently of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\), and this leads to the Student’s \(t\) distribution. Proposition 8.5 (Student's t Distribution for a Linear Combination) Consider the linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, the model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Let \[ \nu=n-p-1 \] denote the residual degrees of freedom. For any fixed nonzero vector \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}\), \[ T_{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } } \] satisfies \[ T_{\mathbf{a}}\sim t_\nu. \] Proof Proof. Since \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right), \] we have \[ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} \right). \] Therefore, \[ Z_{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} }{ \sigma \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } } \sim N(0,1). \] From the distribution of the residual variance estimator, \[ \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_\nu. \] Let \[ W = \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2}. \] Then \[ W\sim\chi^2_\nu. \] Furthermore, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) are independent. Therefore, \(Z_{\mathbf{a}}\) and \(W\) are independent. We can now write \[\begin{align*} T_{\mathbf{a}} &= \frac{ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } } \\ &= \frac{ \frac{ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} }{ \sigma \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } } }{ \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2}} } \\ &= \frac{ Z_{\mathbf{a}} }{ \sqrt{\frac{W}{\nu}} }. \end{align*}\] Since \(Z_{\mathbf{a}}\sim N(0,1)\), \(W\sim\chi^2_\nu\), and \(Z_{\mathbf{a}}\) and \(W\) are independent, the definition of the Student’s \(t\) distribution gives \[ T_{\mathbf{a}}\sim t_\nu. \] This result is important because the unknown \(\sigma^2\) has disappeared from the distribution of \(T_{\mathbf{a}}\). The statistic depends only on observable quantities and the unknown linear combination \(\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}\) that we want to estimate. We can now use this result to construct a confidence interval. Proposition 8.6 (Confidence Interval for a Linear Combination) Under the assumptions of Proposition 8.5, a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is \[ \left( \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} }, \; \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} + t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } \right), \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Proof Proof. Since \[ T_{\mathbf{a}}\sim t_\nu, \] and \(t_{\nu,\alpha/2}\) is the upper-tail \(\alpha/2\) quantile, \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{P} \left( -t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \leq T_{\mathbf{a}} \leq t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \right) &= 1-\alpha \\ % \implies \mathbb{P} \left( -t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \leq \frac{ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } } \leq t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \right) &= 1-\alpha \\ % \implies \mathbb{P} \left( -t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } \leq \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} \right. \qquad &\\ \left. \leq t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } \right) &= 1-\alpha \\ % \implies \mathbb{P} \left( \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } \leq \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} \right. \qquad &\\ \left. \leq \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} + t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } \right) &= 1-\alpha. \end{align*}\] Therefore, the corresponding random interval contains \(\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}\) with probability \(1-\alpha\). The proposition provides a general interval-estimation result. Several important confidence intervals in linear regression follow simply by choosing an appropriate vector \(\mathbf{a}\). 8.3.3 Confidence Intervals for Individual Coefficients To obtain a confidence interval for a particular coefficient \(\beta_j\), let \(\mathbf{a}\) be the vector whose \(j\)-th entry is equal to \(1\) and whose remaining entries are equal to \(0\). Then \[ \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}=\beta_j \] and \[ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\hat{\beta}_j. \] Furthermore, \[ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} = [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}. \] Therefore, a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is \[ \boxed{ \left( \hat{\beta}_j - t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} }, \; \hat{\beta}_j + t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } \right), } \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] The width of this interval depends on two different sources of uncertainty. The quantity \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) estimates the variability in the errors, while \[ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} \] depends on the geometry of the explanatory variables. Thus, the relationships among the explanatory variables that affected the variability of the OLS estimator in the previous chapter also directly affect the precision of the corresponding confidence intervals. 8.3.4 Confidence Interval for the Expected Response Suppose that we are interested in the expected response associated with a fixed predictor vector \[ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}, \] where \(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}\) includes the intercept entry. Under the regression model, \[ \mu_{\mathrm{new}} = \mathbb{E}[y_{\mathrm{new}}] = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta}. \] Its natural estimator is \[ \hat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] This is another linear combination of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Therefore, we can apply the previous proposition using \[ \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}. \] A \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for the expected response is \[ \boxed{ \left( \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} }, \; \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} + t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} } \right). } \] This interval quantifies uncertainty about the mean response \[ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta}. \] It does not quantify uncertainty about a future individual response. A future observation contains an additional random error that is not present when estimating the mean response. 8.3.5 Prediction Interval for a New Observation Suppose now that a new observation is generated at the predictor vector \(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}\) according to \[ y_{\mathrm{new}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta} + e_{\mathrm{new}}, \] where \[ e_{\mathrm{new}}\sim N(0,\sigma^2) \] and \(e_{\mathrm{new}}\) is independent of the errors used to fit the regression model. The natural prediction of \(y_{\mathrm{new}}\) is \[ \hat{y}_{\mathrm{new}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] The prediction error is \[\begin{align*} y_{\mathrm{new}} - \hat{y}_{\mathrm{new}} &= \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta} + e_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \\ &= e_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}). \end{align*}\] The two terms on the right are independent. Therefore, \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{V} \left[ y_{\mathrm{new}} - \hat{y}_{\mathrm{new}} \right] &= \mathbb{V}[e_{\mathrm{new}}] + \mathbb{V} \left[ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}) \right] \\ &= \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} \\ &= \sigma^2 \left( 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} \right). \end{align*}\] Proposition 8.7 (Prediction Interval for a New Observation) Consider the Normal linear regression model with \(\mathbf{X}\) of full column rank, \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept. Suppose that \[ y_{\mathrm{new}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta}+e_{\mathrm{new}}, \] where \[ e_{\mathrm{new}}\sim N(0,\sigma^2) \] and \(e_{\mathrm{new}}\) is independent of the data used to fit the model. Then \[ \frac{ y_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} } } \sim t_\nu, \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Consequently, a \((1-\alpha)\) prediction interval for \(y_{\mathrm{new}}\) is \[ \boxed{ \left( \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} - t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} }, \; \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} + t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} } \right). } \] Proof Proof. Since \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is multivariate Normal and \(e_{\mathrm{new}}\) is an independent Normal random variable, \[ y_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \] is normally distributed. Its expectation is \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \left[ y_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \right] &= \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] + \mathbb{E}[e_{\mathrm{new}}] \\ &= 0. \end{align*}\] Its variance is \[ \sigma^2 \left( 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} \right). \] Therefore, \[ Z_{\mathrm{new}} = \frac{ y_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} }{ \sigma \sqrt{ 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} } } \sim N(0,1). \] Furthermore, \[ \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_\nu. \] The new error \(e_{\mathrm{new}}\) is independent of the data used to construct \(\hat{\sigma}^2\), and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is independent of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). Therefore, \(Z_{\mathrm{new}}\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) are independent. It follows that \[ \frac{ Z_{\mathrm{new}} }{ \sqrt{ \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2/\sigma^2}{\nu} } } = \frac{ y_{\mathrm{new}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} } } \sim t_\nu. \] Using the upper-tail quantile \(t_{\nu,\alpha/2}\) and proceeding as in the confidence interval for a linear combination gives the stated prediction interval. The distinction between the confidence interval for the mean response and the prediction interval is important. Both intervals are centered at \[ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \] but their estimated variances are different: \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} \] for estimation of the mean response, and \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \left( 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) \] for prediction of a new observation. The additional \(1\) represents the variability of the new error \(e_{\mathrm{new}}\). Therefore, for the same \(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}\) and confidence level, the prediction interval is wider than the confidence interval for the mean response. 8.3.6 Confidence Interval for \(\sigma^2\) The chi-squared distribution obtained in the previous section also allows us to construct an interval estimator for the error variance itself. Recall that \[ \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_\nu, \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Using the upper-tail quantile notation introduced earlier, \[ \mathbb{P} \left( \chi^2_{\nu,1-\alpha/2} \leq \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \leq \chi^2_{\nu,\alpha/2} \right) = 1-\alpha. \] Solving the inequalities for \(\sigma^2\) gives \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{P} \left( \chi^2_{\nu,1-\alpha/2} \leq \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \leq \chi^2_{\nu,\alpha/2} \right) &= 1-\alpha \\ % \implies \mathbb{P} \left( \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2} {\chi^2_{\nu,\alpha/2}} \leq \sigma^2 \leq \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2} {\chi^2_{\nu,1-\alpha/2}} \right) &= 1-\alpha. \end{align*}\] Therefore, a \((1-\alpha)\) confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) is \[ \boxed{ \left( \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2} {\chi^2_{\nu,\alpha/2}}, \; \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2} {\chi^2_{\nu,1-\alpha/2}} \right). } \] Unlike the confidence intervals for linear combinations of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), this interval is generally not symmetric around \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). This follows from the asymmetry of the chi-squared distribution. The interval estimators developed in this section all arise from the same general strategy. We begin with a statistic whose sampling distribution is known and whose distribution does not depend on unknown quantities after appropriate standardization. We then use distributional quantiles to obtain a probability statement and solve that statement for the unknown quantity of interest. The same sampling distributions will be used in the next section from a different perspective. Rather than constructing a range of plausible parameter values, we will assume a particular parameter value under a null hypothesis and determine whether the observed data are consistent with that assumption. 8.4 Hypothesis Testing The sampling distributions derived in the previous sections allow us to address another inferential question. Instead of constructing a range of plausible values for an unknown parameter, suppose that we want to evaluate a particular statement about the regression model. We will approach hypothesis testing using an implausibility framework. We begin by specifying a null hypothesis, denoted by \(\mathcal{H}_0\), and temporarily assume that it is true. We then construct a statistic whose sampling distribution is known conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\). After observing the data, we compare the observed value of the statistic with its distribution under the null hypothesis. If the observed value would be unusually extreme conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), this provides evidence against the null hypothesis. Throughout this section, notation such as \[ \mathbb{P}(A\mid\mathcal{H}_0) \] will denote the probability of the event \(A\) calculated using the sampling distribution implied by the null hypothesis. This notation does not mean that \(\mathcal{H}_0\) is being treated as a random event. Instead, it emphasizes that the relevant probability distribution is obtained by assuming that the parameter restrictions specified by \(\mathcal{H}_0\) are true. This reasoning leads to the concept of a \(p\)-value. Definition 8.2 (p-value) The \(p\)-value is the probability, computed conditional on the null hypothesis, of obtaining a value of the test statistic at least as extreme as the value observed in the data, where the meaning of “extreme” is determined by the alternative hypothesis. Thus, if \(T^*\) denotes the observed value of a test statistic \(T\), the \(p\)-value has the general form \[ \mathbb{P} \left( T\text{ is at least as extreme as }T^* \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right). \] A small \(p\)-value indicates that the observed statistic would be unusual under the sampling distribution implied by \(\mathcal{H}_0\). Given a significance level \(\alpha\), we reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\) when \[ p\text{-value}\leq\alpha. \] Otherwise, we do not reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\). Notice that \[ \mathbb{P}(\text{data as or more extreme}\mid\mathcal{H}_0) \] is not the same quantity as \[ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_0\mid\text{data}). \] The hypothesis-testing framework developed here concerns the first probability. Many important hypothesis tests in linear regression can be understood as comparisons between two nested regression models. We will first develop this general result and then use it to construct tests for the overall regression and for groups of explanatory variables. 8.4.1 Comparing Nested Regression Models Suppose that we have a full regression model with design matrix \(\mathbf{X}_F\) and a reduced regression model with design matrix \(\mathbf{X}_R\), where \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_F). \] Thus, every response pattern that can be represented by the reduced model can also be represented by the full model. Let \[ \mathbf{H}_F = \mathbf{X}_F(\mathbf{X}_F'\mathbf{X}_F)^{-1}\mathbf{X}_F' \] and \[ \mathbf{H}_R = \mathbf{X}_R(\mathbf{X}_R'\mathbf{X}_R)^{-1}\mathbf{X}_R' \] be the corresponding projection matrices, assuming both design matrices have full column rank. The residual sums of squares are \[ SS_{res,F} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F)\mathbf{y} \] and \[ SS_{res,R} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{y}. \] Since the full model contains all the directions available to the reduced model, fitting the full model cannot increase the residual sum of squares. The quantity \[ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} \] therefore measures the reduction in residual variation obtained by moving from the reduced model to the full model. The following proposition determines the distribution of this reduction conditional on the null hypothesis that the reduced model is sufficient. Proposition 8.8 (F Test for Nested Regression Models) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Let \(\mathbf{X}_F\) and \(\mathbf{X}_R\) be full-column-rank design matrices satisfying \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_F), \] with corresponding projection matrices \(\mathbf{H}_F\) and \(\mathbf{H}_R\). Let \[ r_F=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_F), \qquad r_R=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}_R), \] and define \[ q=r_F-r_R, \qquad \nu=n-r_F. \] Under the null hypothesis \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R), \] the statistic \[ F = \frac{ \frac{SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F}}{q} }{ \frac{SS_{res,F}}{\nu} } \] satisfies \[ F\mid\mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{q,\nu}. \] Proof Proof. We begin by studying the relationship between the two projection matrices. Since \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_F), \] every vector in \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R)\) is unchanged when projected onto \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_F)\). Therefore, \[ \mathbf{H}_F\mathbf{H}_R=\mathbf{H}_R. \] Taking transposes and using the symmetry of both projection matrices, \[\begin{align*} (\mathbf{H}_F\mathbf{H}_R)' &= \mathbf{H}_R'\mathbf{H}_F' \\ &= \mathbf{H}_R\mathbf{H}_F \end{align*}\] and \[ (\mathbf{H}_F\mathbf{H}_R)' = \mathbf{H}_R'. \] Therefore, \[ \mathbf{H}_R\mathbf{H}_F = \mathbf{H}_R. \] Now consider \[ \mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R. \] Since both matrices are symmetric, their difference is symmetric. Furthermore, \[\begin{align*} (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)^2 &= \mathbf{H}_F\mathbf{H}_F - \mathbf{H}_F\mathbf{H}_R - \mathbf{H}_R\mathbf{H}_F + \mathbf{H}_R\mathbf{H}_R \\ &= \mathbf{H}_F - \mathbf{H}_R - \mathbf{H}_R + \mathbf{H}_R && \text{since $\mathbf{H}_F$ and $\mathbf{H}_R$ are idempotent} \\ &= \mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R. \end{align*}\] Thus, \(\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R\) is symmetric and idempotent. Its rank can be obtained from its trace: \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R) &= \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R) && \text{since $\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R$ is idempotent} \\ &= \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}_F) - \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}_R) \\ &= r_F-r_R \\ &= q. \end{align*}\] Next, \[\begin{align*} SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F)\mathbf{y}\\ &= \mathbf{y}' \left[ (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_R)-(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F) \right] \mathbf{y}\\ &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{y}. \end{align*}\] Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[ \boldsymbol{\mu}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R). \] Therefore, \[ \mathbf{H}_R\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\mu} \] and \[ \mathbf{H}_F\boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\mu}. \] It follows that \[ (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0}. \] Since \[ \mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{e}, \] we obtain, conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[\begin{align*} (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{y} &= (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R) (\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{e}) \\ &= (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\boldsymbol{\mu} + (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{e}\\ &= (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{e}. \end{align*}\] Consequently, \[ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} = \mathbf{e}'(\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{e} \qquad \text{under $\mathcal{H}_0$}. \] Since \[ \frac{\mathbf{e}}{\sigma} \sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), \] and \(\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R\) is symmetric and idempotent with rank \(q\), Proposition 8.2 gives \[ \left. \frac{ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} }{ \sigma^2 } \right| \mathcal{H}_0 \sim \chi^2_q. \] Similarly, \[ (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F)\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0} \] under \(\mathcal{H}_0\), and \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F\) is symmetric and idempotent with rank \[ n-r_F=\nu. \] Therefore, \[ \left. \frac{SS_{res,F}}{\sigma^2} \right| \mathcal{H}_0 \sim \chi^2_\nu. \] It remains to establish independence. Consider \[ (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{y} \] and \[ (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F)\mathbf{y}. \] Their cross-covariance is \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{C}[ (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R)\mathbf{y}, (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F)\mathbf{y} ] &= (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R) \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{y}] (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F) \\ &= \sigma^2 (\mathbf{H}_F-\mathbf{H}_R) (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_F) \\ &= \mathbf{0}. \end{align*}\] Both vectors are jointly Normal because they are linear transformations of \(\mathbf{y}\). Therefore, they are independent. Consequently, \[ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} \] and \[ SS_{res,F} \] are independent. We have therefore established, conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[ \frac{ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} }{ \sigma^2 } \sim \chi^2_q, \] \[ \frac{ SS_{res,F} }{ \sigma^2 } \sim \chi^2_\nu, \] with the two quantities independent. Hence, \[\begin{align*} F &= \frac{ \frac{SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F}}{q} }{ \frac{SS_{res,F}}{\nu} } \\ &= \frac{ \frac{1}{q} \frac{SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F}}{\sigma^2} }{ \frac{1}{\nu} \frac{SS_{res,F}}{\sigma^2} } \\ &\sim \frac{ \chi^2_q/q }{ \chi^2_\nu/\nu } \\ &\sim F_{q,\nu}, \end{align*}\] conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\). The numerator measures the improvement in fit obtained by moving from the reduced model to the full model. The denominator estimates the error variance using the residual variation remaining in the full model. Thus, the \(F\) statistic compares \[ \text{variation explained by the additional model components} \] with \[ \text{unexplained variation remaining in the full model}. \] Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), the additional directions in the full model represent no systematic component of the mean. Any improvement in fit produced by them is therefore attributable to random variation. An unusually large improvement provides evidence against \(\mathcal{H}_0\). 8.4.2 Testing the Overall Regression We can now apply the nested-model result to test whether the explanatory variables collectively contribute to the regression model. Recall that \[ \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{1}\;\mathbf{X}_*], \] where \(\mathbf{X}_*\) contains the \(p\) explanatory variables. The coefficient vector is \[ \boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p)'. \] The null hypothesis is \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \beta_1=\cdots=\beta_p=0. \] Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] = \beta_0\mathbf{1}. \] Thus, the reduced model is the intercept-only model. Its projection matrix is \[ \mathbf{H}_0 = \mathbf{1}(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1})^{-1}\mathbf{1}'. \] The residual sum of squares for the reduced model is \[ \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y} = SS_{tot}, \] while for the full model, \[ SS_{res} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}. \] Therefore, \[\begin{align*} SS_{tot}-SS_{res} &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}\\ &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}\\ &= SS_{reg}. \end{align*}\] The full model has rank \(p+1\), while the intercept-only model has rank \(1\). Thus, \[ q=p \] and \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Proposition 8.9 (Overall Regression F Test) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \[ \mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{1}\;\mathbf{X}_*] \] has full column rank, \(\mathbf{X}_*\) contains \(p\) explanatory variables, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Under \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \beta_1=\cdots=\beta_p=0, \] the statistic \[ F_{\mathrm{overall}} = \frac{ SS_{reg}/p }{ SS_{res}/(n-p-1) } \] satisfies \[ F_{\mathrm{overall}} \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{p,n-p-1}. \] Proof Proof. Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), the reduced model is the intercept-only model, whose column space is \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{1}). \] Since \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{1}) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}), \] the two models are nested. Furthermore, \[ SS_{res,R}=SS_{tot}, \] \[ SS_{res,F}=SS_{res}, \] and \[ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F}=SS_{reg}. \] The difference in ranks is \[ q=(p+1)-1=p, \] and the residual degrees of freedom are \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Therefore, Proposition 8.8 gives \[ F_{\mathrm{overall}} \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{p,n-p-1}. \] Once the data are observed, let \[ F_{\mathrm{overall}}^* \] denote the observed value. Since large values provide evidence against the intercept-only model, the \(p\)-value is \[ \boxed{ \mathbb{P} \left( F_{\mathrm{overall}} \geq F_{\mathrm{overall}}^* \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right). } \] At significance level \(\alpha\), we reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\) when \[ F_{\mathrm{overall}}^* \geq f_{p,n-p-1,\alpha}. \] 8.4.3 Testing a Single Regression Coefficient We may want to determine whether a particular explanatory variable contributes to the regression after accounting for the other variables already included in the model. For the coefficient \(\beta_j\), consider \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \beta_j=0 \] against \[ \mathcal{H}_1: \beta_j\neq0. \] There are two useful ways to understand this test. The first uses the sampling distribution of the coefficient estimator directly. The second treats the test as a comparison between two nested regression models. These approaches lead to exactly the same test. 8.4.3.1 Direct Approach Using the \(t\) Distribution Proposition 8.10 (t Test for a Single Regression Coefficient) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, the model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Under \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \beta_j=0, \] the statistic \[ T_j = \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \] satisfies \[ T_j \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim t_{n-p-1}. \] Proof Proof. Let \(\mathbf{a}\) be the vector with a \(1\) in the position corresponding to \(\beta_j\) and zeros elsewhere. Then \[ \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} = \beta_j \] and \[ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \hat{\beta}_j. \] From Proposition 8.5, \[ \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j-\beta_j }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \sim t_{n-p-1}. \] Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[ \beta_j=0. \] Therefore, \[ T_j = \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim t_{n-p-1}. \] Once the data are observed, let \(T_j^*\) denote the observed value. Since the alternative is two-sided, values sufficiently far from zero in either direction provide evidence against \(\mathcal{H}_0\). The \(p\)-value is therefore \[ \boxed{ 2\mathbb{P} \left( T_j \geq |T_j^*| \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right), } \] where the probability is evaluated using the \(t_{n-p-1}\) distribution. Equivalently, we reject at significance level \(\alpha\) when \[ |T_j^*| \geq t_{n-p-1,\alpha/2}. \] 8.4.3.2 Nested-Model Interpretation The same hypothesis can also be interpreted geometrically as a comparison between two nested regression models. Write the complete design matrix as \[ \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{x}_j\;\mathbf{X}_{-j}], \] where \(\mathbf{x}_j\) is the column associated with \(\beta_j\) and \(\mathbf{X}_{-j}\) contains all remaining columns of the design matrix, including the intercept. The full model is \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}_j\beta_j + \mathbf{X}_{-j}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-j} + \mathbf{e}. \] Under \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \beta_j=0, \] the model reduces to \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_{-j}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{-j} + \mathbf{e}. \] Thus, testing a single coefficient is also a nested-model comparison in which the full model contains exactly one additional direction. Let \[ \mathbf{H}_{-j} \] denote the projection matrix onto \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_{-j})\), and define \[ \mathbf{M}_{-j} = \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_{-j}. \] The vector \[ \mathbf{z}_j = \mathbf{M}_{-j}\mathbf{x}_j \] is the component of \(\mathbf{x}_j\) that cannot be explained by the remaining columns of the design matrix. Because \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, \[ \mathbf{z}_j\neq\mathbf{0}. \] Furthermore, \[ \mathbf{z}_j \perp \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_{-j}). \] Since \[ \mathbf{x}_j = \mathbf{H}_{-j}\mathbf{x}_j+\mathbf{z}_j, \] adding \(\mathbf{x}_j\) to the reduced model adds exactly the new direction generated by \(\mathbf{z}_j\). Consequently, \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_{-j}) \oplus \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{z}_j). \] Therefore, \[ \mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_{-j} = \mathbf{z}_j(\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j)^{-1}\mathbf{z}_j'. \] This matrix projects onto the single additional direction contributed by \(\mathbf{x}_j\) after accounting for all the other explanatory variables. The reduction in residual sum of squares obtained by adding \(\mathbf{x}_j\) is \[\begin{align*} SS_{res,-j}-SS_{res} &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_{-j})\mathbf{y}\\ &= \mathbf{y}' \mathbf{z}_j(\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j)^{-1}\mathbf{z}_j' \mathbf{y}\\ &= \frac{ (\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{y})^2 }{ \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j }. \end{align*}\] We can connect this quantity directly to \(\hat{\beta}_j\). Since the least squares residual is orthogonal to every column of \(\mathbf{X}\), it is also orthogonal to \(\mathbf{z}_j\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\). Thus, \[\begin{align*} 0 &= \mathbf{z}_j'\hat{\mathbf{e}} \\ &= \mathbf{z}_j' \left( \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}_j\hat{\beta}_j - \mathbf{X}_{-j}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-j} \right) \\ &= \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{y} - \hat{\beta}_j\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{x}_j && \text{since $\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{X}_{-j}=\mathbf{0}$}. \end{align*}\] Also, \[\begin{align*} \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{x}_j &= \mathbf{z}_j' (\mathbf{H}_{-j}\mathbf{x}_j+\mathbf{z}_j) \\ &= \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j && \text{since $\mathbf{z}_j\perp\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_{-j})$}. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[ \hat{\beta}_j = \frac{ \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{y} }{ \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j }. \] It follows that \[\begin{align*} SS_{res,-j}-SS_{res} &= \frac{ (\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{y})^2 }{ \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j } \\ &= \hat{\beta}_j^2 (\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j). \end{align*}\] We also know that \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\beta}_j] = \sigma^2 [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}. \] From \[ \hat{\beta}_j = \frac{\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j}, \] we can compute \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{V}[\hat{\beta}_j] &= \frac{ \mathbf{z}_j'\mathbb{V}[\mathbf{y}]\mathbf{z}_j }{ (\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j)^2 } \\ &= \frac{ \sigma^2\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j }{ (\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j)^2 } \\ &= \frac{\sigma^2}{\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j}. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{z}_j'\mathbf{z}_j}. \] Substituting this result, \[ SS_{res,-j}-SS_{res} = \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j^2 }{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} }. \] The nested-model \(F\) statistic is therefore \[\begin{align*} F_j &= \frac{ SS_{res,-j}-SS_{res} }{ SS_{res}/(n-p-1) } \\ &= \frac{ \frac{\hat{\beta}_j^2} {[(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}} }{ \hat{\sigma}^2 } \\ &= \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j^2 }{ \hat{\sigma}^2 [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } \\ &= T_j^2. \end{align*}\] Thus, \[ \boxed{ F_j=T_j^2. } \] Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), the nested-model result gives \[ F_j\mid\mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{1,n-p-1}, \] while the direct approach gives \[ T_j\mid\mathcal{H}_0 \sim t_{n-p-1}. \] These results are consistent because the square of a Student \(t\) random variable with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom follows an \(F\) distribution with \(1\) and \(\nu\) degrees of freedom: \[ T_j^2 \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{1,n-p-1}. \] The two approaches therefore produce exactly the same test. The direct \(t\) approach focuses on the estimated coefficient relative to its standard error: \[ \frac{\text{estimated coefficient}} {\text{estimated standard deviation of the coefficient}}. \] The nested-model approach focuses on the reduction in residual variation produced by adding that explanatory variable: \[ \frac{ \text{improvement in fit from adding the variable} }{ \text{remaining residual variation} }. \] The equality \[ F_j=T_j^2 \] shows that these are two representations of the same underlying information. In particular, the two-sided \(t\)-test and the one-variable partial \(F\)-test produce the same \(p\)-value: \[ \mathbb{P} \left( F_j\geq (T_j^*)^2 \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right) = \mathbb{P} \left( |T_j|\geq|T_j^*| \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right). \] This also clarifies what it means to test whether a single explanatory variable contributes to the model. The question is not whether \(\mathbf{x}_j\) is related to the response in isolation. Rather, it is whether the component of \(\mathbf{x}_j\) that cannot already be represented by the remaining explanatory variables contributes additional information about the mean response. 8.4.4 Testing a Subgroup of Regression Coefficients The overall regression test considers all explanatory variables simultaneously, while the individual coefficient test considers one additional direction. Between these cases, we may want to test whether a group of explanatory variables contributes to the model after accounting for the remaining variables. Suppose \[ \mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{X}_1\;\mathbf{X}_2], \] where \(\mathbf{X}_1\) contains the \(k\) explanatory variables to be tested and \(\mathbf{X}_2\) contains the remaining variables, including the intercept. Partition \[ \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\beta}_1\\ \boldsymbol{\beta}_2 \end{pmatrix}. \] The full model is \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\beta}_1 + \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2 + \mathbf{e}. \] We test \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}. \] Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] = \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2. \] Thus, the reduced model contains only \(\mathbf{X}_2\). Let \[ \mathbf{H}_2 = \mathbf{X}_2(\mathbf{X}_2'\mathbf{X}_2)^{-1}\mathbf{X}_2' \] and \[ SS_{res,2} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbf{y}. \] The improvement from adding \(\mathbf{X}_1\) is \[\begin{align*} SS_{res,2}-SS_{res} &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}\\ &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbf{y}. \end{align*}\] Proposition 8.11 (Partial F Test for a Subgroup of Regression Coefficients) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\beta}_1 + \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2 + \mathbf{e}, \] where \[ \mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{X}_1\;\mathbf{X}_2] \] has full column rank, \(\mathbf{X}_1\) contains \(k\) explanatory variables, the complete model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Under \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}, \] the statistic \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} = \frac{ (SS_{res,2}-SS_{res})/k }{ SS_{res}/(n-p-1) } \] satisfies \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{k,n-p-1}. \] Proof Proof. Conditional on \(\mathcal{H}_0\), \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] = \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2. \] Thus, the reduced model has design matrix \(\mathbf{X}_2\), while the full model has design matrix \[ \mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{X}_1\;\mathbf{X}_2]. \] Since \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_2) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}), \] the models are nested. The difference between their residual sums of squares is \[ SS_{res,2}-SS_{res}. \] Since the full model contains \(k\) additional linearly independent columns, \[ q=k. \] The complete design matrix has rank \(p+1\), so \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Applying Proposition 8.8, \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{k,n-p-1}. \] Once the data are observed, let \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}}^* \] denote the observed value. The \(p\)-value is \[ \boxed{ \mathbb{P} \left( F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \geq F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}}^* \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right). } \] At significance level \(\alpha\), we reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\) when \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}}^* \geq f_{k,n-p-1,\alpha}. \] The overall regression test, the single-coefficient test, and the subgroup test can therefore all be understood through the same nested-model structure. For the overall regression, \[ \text{reduced model} = \text{intercept only}. \] For a single coefficient, \[ \text{reduced model} = \text{full model with one explanatory variable removed}. \] For a subgroup, \[ \text{reduced model} = \text{full model with the tested group removed}. \] In every case, the null hypothesis specifies that the reduced model is sufficient to represent the mean response. The test asks whether the improvement obtained by enlarging the model is unusually large conditional on that assumption. Thus, the common question behind these tests is \[ \boxed{ \text{Is the improvement produced by the additional model components too large to be plausibly attributed to random variation under }\mathcal{H}_0\text{?} } \] The Normality assumption allows this question to be answered exactly through the \(t\) and \(F\) sampling distributions. 8.5 Power Analysis In the previous section, we constructed hypothesis tests by first assuming that a null hypothesis \(\mathcal{H}_0\) is true and then determining the sampling distribution of a test statistic conditional on that assumption. For example, for a particular regression coefficient we obtained \[ T_j\mid\mathcal{H}_0 \sim t_{n-p-1}, \] while for a subgroup of \(k\) coefficients we obtained \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}}\mid\mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{k,n-p-1}. \] These distributions allowed us to choose rejection regions with a prescribed probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is true. However, once a hypothesis test has been constructed, another question naturally arises: If the null hypothesis is false, how likely is the test to detect that it is false? This question is answered through the power of a hypothesis test. 8.5.1 Type I Error, Type II Error, and Power Consider a test of \[ \mathcal{H}_0 \] against an alternative \[ \mathcal{H}_1. \] There are two possible decisions: reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\) or do not reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\). Since the true parameter values are unknown, either decision can be correct or incorrect. A Type I error occurs when we reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\) even though \(\mathcal{H}_0\) is true. The significance level \(\alpha\) controls the probability of this error: \[ \mathbb{P} \left( \text{reject }\mathcal{H}_0 \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right) = \alpha. \] A Type II error occurs when we do not reject \(\mathcal{H}_0\) even though a particular alternative is true. If \(\theta\) denotes a parameter value under the alternative, we can write the probability of a Type II error as \[ \beta_{\mathrm{II}}(\theta) = \mathbb{P} \left( \text{do not reject }\mathcal{H}_0 \mid \theta \right). \] The corresponding power is the probability that the test correctly rejects the null hypothesis under that alternative. Definition 8.3 (Power of a Hypothesis Test) Let \(\theta\) denote a particular parameter value under the alternative hypothesis. The power of a hypothesis test at \(\theta\) is \[ \pi(\theta) = \mathbb{P} \left( \text{reject }\mathcal{H}_0 \mid \theta \right). \] Equivalently, \[ \pi(\theta) = 1-\beta_{\mathrm{II}}(\theta). \] Thus, the significance level and the power answer different conditional probability questions: \[ \alpha = \mathbb{P} \left( \text{reject }\mathcal{H}_0 \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \right), \] while \[ \pi(\theta) = \mathbb{P} \left( \text{reject }\mathcal{H}_0 \mid \theta \right) \] for a specified alternative \(\theta\). The rejection region itself does not change between these calculations. What changes is the distribution of the test statistic. The rejection region is constructed using the distribution under \(\mathcal{H}_0\), while power is calculated using the distribution under the alternative. To determine power in the Normal linear regression model, we therefore need to understand how the \(t\) and \(F\) statistics behave when the null hypothesis is false. 8.5.2 Noncentral \(t\) and \(F\) Distributions The central \(t\) and \(F\) distributions used for hypothesis testing are particular cases of more general distributions. Definition 8.4 (Noncentral t Distribution) Suppose that \[ Z\sim N(\delta,1) \] and \[ W\sim\chi^2_\nu \] are independent. Then \[ T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{W/\nu}} \] has a noncentral Student’s \(t\) distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter \(\delta\). We denote this by \[ T\sim t_\nu(\delta). \] When \[ \delta=0, \] the noncentral \(t\) distribution reduces to the usual central Student’s \(t\) distribution: \[ t_\nu(0)=t_\nu. \] The same idea extends to the \(F\) distribution. Definition 8.5 (Noncentral F Distribution) Suppose that \[ U\sim\chi^2_q(\lambda) \] has a noncentral chi-squared distribution with \(q\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\), and suppose that \[ W\sim\chi^2_\nu \] is independent of \(U\).
