Then \[ F = \frac{U/q}{W/\nu} \] has a noncentral \(F\) distribution with \(q\) and \(\nu\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\). We denote this by \[ F\sim F_{q,\nu}(\lambda). \] When \[ \lambda=0, \] the noncentral \(F\) distribution reduces to the usual central \(F\) distribution: \[ F_{q,\nu}(0)=F_{q,\nu}. \] The noncentrality parameters \(\delta\) and \(\lambda\) measure how far the true model is from the corresponding null hypothesis, relative to the variability in the model. We can now use these distributions to compute the power of the regression tests developed previously. 8.5.3 Power for Testing a Single Regression Coefficient Consider again the two-sided test \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \beta_j=0 \] against \[ \mathcal{H}_1: \beta_j\neq0. \] The test statistic is \[ T_j = \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }. \] Under the null hypothesis, \[ T_j\mid\mathcal{H}_0 \sim t_\nu, \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] At significance level \(\alpha\), the rejection region is \[ |T_j| \geq t_{\nu,\alpha/2}. \] The rejection region is determined entirely from the distribution under \(\mathcal{H}_0\). To calculate power, however, suppose that the true coefficient is some particular value \[ \beta_j=\theta, \qquad \theta\neq0. \] The distribution of \(T_j\) changes. Proposition 8.12 (Distribution of the t Statistic Under an Alternative) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, the model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] For the statistic \[ T_j = \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }, \] if \[ \beta_j=\theta, \] then \[ T_j \mid \beta_j=\theta \sim t_\nu(\delta_j), \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1 \] and \[ \boxed{ \delta_j = \frac{ \theta }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }. } \] Proof Proof. From the sampling distribution of the least squares estimator, \[ \hat{\beta}_j \sim N \left( \beta_j, \sigma^2[(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} \right). \] Therefore, conditional on \[ \beta_j=\theta, \] we have \[ \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \sim N \left( \frac{ \theta }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }, 1 \right). \] Define \[ \delta_j = \frac{ \theta }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }. \] Then \[ Z_j = \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \sim N(\delta_j,1). \] Furthermore, \[ \frac{\nu\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_\nu, \] and \(\hat{\beta}_j\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) are independent. Therefore, \[\begin{align*} T_j &= \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \\ &= \frac{ \frac{ \hat{\beta}_j }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } }{ \sqrt{ \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} } } \\ &= \frac{ Z_j }{ \sqrt{ \frac{ \nu\hat{\sigma}^2/\sigma^2 }{ \nu } } }. \end{align*}\] The numerator is \(N(\delta_j,1)\), the quantity in the denominator is obtained from an independent \(\chi^2_\nu\) random variable, and therefore \[ T_j \mid \beta_j=\theta \sim t_\nu(\delta_j). \] The power of the two-sided test at \(\beta_j=\theta\) is therefore the probability that a noncentral \(t\) random variable falls in the rejection region: \[ \boxed{ \pi_j(\theta) = \mathbb{P} \left( |T_j| \geq t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \mid \beta_j=\theta \right). } \] Equivalently, \[\begin{align*} \pi_j(\theta) &= \mathbb{P} \left( T_j \leq -t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \mid \beta_j=\theta \right) \\ &\quad+ \mathbb{P} \left( T_j \geq t_{\nu,\alpha/2} \mid \beta_j=\theta \right). \end{align*}\] When \[ \theta=0, \] we have \[ \delta_j=0. \] The noncentral \(t\) distribution then becomes the central \(t\) distribution, and \[ \pi_j(0) = \alpha. \] This is precisely the probability of a Type I error. As \(\theta\) moves away from zero, the distribution of the test statistic moves away from the distribution specified by the null hypothesis. Consequently, it becomes more likely for \(T_j\) to fall in the rejection region. The noncentrality parameter \[ |\delta_j| = \frac{ |\theta| }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } } \] provides a useful interpretation of power. Power increases when the magnitude of the alternative coefficient increases relative to the uncertainty with which that coefficient can be estimated. A larger error standard deviation \(\sigma\) makes the effect more difficult to detect. The design matrix also plays an important role through \[ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}. \] Recall that \[ \mathbb{V}[\hat{\beta}_j] = \sigma^2 [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}. \] Thus, properties of the explanatory variables that increase the variance of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) also decrease the magnitude of the noncentrality parameter and therefore decrease the ability of the test to distinguish \(\beta_j=\theta\) from \(\beta_j=0\). In particular, the effects of cross-correlation among explanatory variables that we studied previously affect not only the precision of coefficient estimates and the width of confidence intervals, but also the power of hypothesis tests. 8.5.4 Power for Testing a Subgroup of Regression Coefficients Now consider the partitioned regression model \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\beta}_1 + \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2 + \mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}_1\) contains the \(k\) explanatory variables to be tested and \(\mathbf{X}_2\) contains the remaining variables, including the intercept. We test \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}. \] The partial \(F\) statistic is \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} = \frac{ (SS_{res,2}-SS_{res})/k }{ SS_{res}/\nu }, \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Under the null hypothesis, \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \mid \mathcal{H}_0 \sim F_{k,\nu}. \] At significance level \(\alpha\), we reject when \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \geq f_{k,\nu,\alpha}. \] Suppose now that the true value of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_1\) is \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta}, \] where \[ \boldsymbol{\theta}\neq\mathbf{0}. \] To determine the distribution of the statistic under this alternative, recall that \[ SS_{res,2}-SS_{res} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbf{y}. \] Unlike under the null hypothesis, the projection \[ (\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}] \] is now generally nonzero. Consequently, the numerator no longer follows a central chi-squared distribution. Let \[ \mathbf{M}_2 = \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2. \] The matrix \(\mathbf{M}_2\) removes from a vector the component that can already be represented by the reduced model. Therefore, \[ \mathbf{M}_2\mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\theta} \] represents the portion of the mean contribution from the variables being tested that cannot be represented by the variables retained in the reduced model. Proposition 8.13 (Distribution of the Partial F Statistic Under an Alternative) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\beta}_1 + \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2 + \mathbf{e}, \] where \[ \mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{X}_1\;\mathbf{X}_2] \] has full column rank, \(\mathbf{X}_1\) contains \(k\) explanatory variables, the complete model contains \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] If \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta}, \] then \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim F_{k,\nu}(\lambda), \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1 \] and \[ \boxed{ \lambda = \frac{ \boldsymbol{\theta}' \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \boldsymbol{\theta} }{ \sigma^2 }. } \] Proof Proof. Let \[ \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_2. \] From the previous section, \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric and idempotent with rank \(k\). The numerator of the partial \(F\) statistic satisfies \[ SS_{res,2}-SS_{res} = \mathbf{y}'\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}. \] Under the alternative \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta}, \] the mean of \(\mathbf{y}\) is \[ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\theta} + \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2. \] Since \[ \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{0}, \] we have \[\begin{align*} \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu} &= \mathbf{A} ( \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\theta} + \mathbf{X}_2\boldsymbol{\beta}_2 ) \\ &= \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\theta}. \end{align*}\] Furthermore, \[\begin{align*} \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}_1 &= (\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbf{X}_1 \\ &= \mathbf{X}_1-\mathbf{H}_2\mathbf{X}_1 \\ &= (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2)\mathbf{X}_1. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[ \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1\boldsymbol{\theta}. \] Since \(\mathbf{y}\) is multivariate Normal, the quadratic form \[ \frac{\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}}{\sigma^2} \] has a noncentral chi-squared distribution with \(k\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter \[ \lambda = \frac{ \boldsymbol{\mu}'\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu} }{ \sigma^2 }. \] Using the previous identities, \[\begin{align*} \boldsymbol{\mu}'\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu} &= \boldsymbol{\theta}' \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \boldsymbol{\theta}. \end{align*}\] Hence, \[ \frac{ SS_{res,2}-SS_{res} }{ \sigma^2 } \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim \chi^2_k(\lambda), \] where \[ \lambda = \frac{ \boldsymbol{\theta}' \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \boldsymbol{\theta} }{ \sigma^2 }. \] The residual sum of squares from the full model still satisfies \[ \frac{SS_{res}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_\nu, \] where \[ \nu=n-p-1. \] Furthermore, \[ SS_{res,2}-SS_{res} \] and \[ SS_{res} \] are independent. Therefore, \[\begin{align*} F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} &= \frac{ (SS_{res,2}-SS_{res})/k }{ SS_{res}/\nu } \\ &\sim \frac{ \chi^2_k(\lambda)/k }{ \chi^2_\nu/\nu } \\ &\sim F_{k,\nu}(\lambda). \end{align*}\] The power against the particular alternative \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta} \] is therefore \[ \boxed{ \pi(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{P} \left( F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \geq f_{k,\nu,\alpha} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta} \right), } \] where \[ F_{\boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\mathbf{0}} \mid \boldsymbol{\beta}_1=\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim F_{k,\nu}(\lambda). \] When \[ \boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathbf{0}, \] the noncentrality parameter becomes \[ \lambda=0, \] so the noncentral \(F\) distribution reduces to the central \(F\) distribution and \[ \pi(\mathbf{0})=\alpha. \] The noncentrality parameter again provides a useful interpretation of power: \[ \lambda = \frac{ \boldsymbol{\theta}' \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \boldsymbol{\theta} }{ \sigma^2 }. \] The matrix \[ \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2 \] removes from the tested explanatory variables the components that can already be represented by the variables in the reduced model. Therefore, \[ \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \] measures the amount of information about the tested effects that remains after accounting for the other explanatory variables. Consequently, power is high when the tested coefficients produce a large component of the mean response that cannot already be explained by the reduced model, relative to the error variance. The overall regression \(F\) test is a special case of this result. In that case, \(\mathbf{X}_1=\mathbf{X}_*\) contains all \(p\) explanatory variables and \(\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{1}\) contains only the intercept. Therefore, the power of the overall regression test can be obtained from the same noncentral \(F\) framework. 8.5.5 Power and the Regression Design The power calculations above show that power in multiple linear regression is determined by more than the numerical size of a regression coefficient. For a single coefficient, the relevant noncentrality parameter is \[ \delta_j = \frac{ \beta_j }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }. \] For a subgroup of coefficients, it is \[ \lambda = \frac{ \boldsymbol{\beta}_1' \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \boldsymbol{\beta}_1 }{ \sigma^2 }. \] In both cases, power is determined by the relationship among three components: \[ \boxed{ \text{effect magnitude}, \qquad \text{error variability}, \qquad \text{information supplied by the design}. } \] This connects power directly with several ideas studied earlier in the course. The design matrix determines the variance of the least squares estimators, and the same geometry therefore determines how easily departures from a null hypothesis can be detected. A test may have low power because the true effect is small, because the errors are highly variable, or because the configuration of the explanatory variables makes the effect difficult to estimate separately from the other effects. Sample size also affects these quantities because collecting additional observations changes the information contained in the design matrix. This creates an important practical question: How many observations are required to obtain a desired probability of detecting an effect of a specified magnitude? That question reverses the power calculation. Instead of taking the design and sample size as given and computing the resulting power, we specify a desired power and determine what sample size or design would be required to achieve it. We will return to this question in the Applications chapter, where power will be used as a tool for study planning and sample-size determination. 8.6 Maximum Likelihood Estimation Throughout the course, we have estimated the regression coefficients using the least squares criterion. Starting from the optimization problem \[ \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})'(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}), \] we obtained the Ordinary Least Squares estimator \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}. \] This construction did not require a probability distribution for the errors. Later assumptions about the mean and variance of the errors allowed us to study properties such as unbiasedness, variance, and the Gauss–Markov result, while the Normality assumption allowed us to obtain exact sampling distributions and perform statistical inference. The Normality assumption also provides a different approach to estimation. Once a complete probability distribution for the observed response has been specified, we can ask which values of the unknown parameters make the observed data most likely under the assumed model. This leads to Maximum Likelihood Estimation. Under the Normal linear regression model, \[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \[ \mathbf{e} \sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}), \] we have \[ \mathbf{y} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Therefore, for an observed response vector \(\mathbf{y}\), the likelihood function of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) and \(\sigma^2\) is \[\begin{align*} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) &= (2\pi)^{-\frac{n}{2}} |\sigma^2\mathbf{I}|^{-\frac12} \exp \left\{ -\frac12 (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})' (\sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1} (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \right\} \\ &= (2\pi)^{-\frac{n}{2}} (\sigma^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}} \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})' (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \right\} \\ &= (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}} \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})' (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \right\}. \end{align*}\] The likelihood contains the same quadratic quantity that appeared in the least squares problem. We will first determine what this implies for estimation of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), and then estimate \(\sigma^2\). 8.6.1 Maximum Likelihood Estimation of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) Proposition 8.14 (Maximum Likelihood Estimator of the Regression Coefficients) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Then the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{MLE} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] Thus, the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) coincides with the Ordinary Least Squares estimator. Proof Proof. For fixed \(\sigma^2\), the likelihood is \[ \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}} \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})' (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \right\}. \] Recall the decomposition \[\begin{align*} (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})' (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) &= (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})' (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}) \\ &= \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}} + 2\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\mathbf{X}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}) + (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})' \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X} (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}) \\ &= \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}} + (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})' \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X} (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}) && \text{since $\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{0}'$}. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[\begin{align*} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) &= (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}} \exp \left\{ -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}} + (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})' \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X} (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}) \right] \right\}. \end{align*}\] For fixed \(\sigma^2\), the quantities \[ (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}} \] and \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}} \] do not depend on \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Since \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, \(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\) is positive definite. Hence, \[ (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta})' \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X} (\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}) \geq0, \] with equality if and only if \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] Since this quantity enters the likelihood with a negative sign, the likelihood is maximized when \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] Therefore, \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{MLE} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}. \] This result provides a second route to the estimator already obtained through least squares. The two approaches begin from different criteria: \[ \text{Least Squares} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{minimize squared discrepancies}, \] while \[ \text{Maximum Likelihood} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{maximize the likelihood of the observed response}. \] Under the Normal linear regression model, they lead to the same estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). This does not mean that Normality is required to obtain the OLS estimator, its unbiasedness, or the Gauss–Markov result. Rather, Normality supplies an additional interpretation of the estimator through the likelihood. 8.6.2 Maximum Likelihood Estimation of \(\sigma^2\) Once the likelihood has been maximized with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\), we can evaluate it at \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \] and maximize the resulting expression with respect to \(\sigma^2\). Proposition 8.15 (Maximum Likelihood Estimator of the Error Variance) Consider the Normal linear regression model \[ \mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e}, \] where \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank and \[ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Then the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is \[ \tilde{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n}. \] Proof Proof. Substituting \[ \boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \] into the likelihood gives \[ \mathcal{L}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}} \exp \left\{ -\frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{2\sigma^2} \right\}. \] Since the logarithm is strictly increasing, maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood: \[\begin{align*} \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) &= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) -\frac{n}{2}\log(\sigma^2) -\frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{2\sigma^2}. \end{align*}\] Differentiating with respect to \(\sigma^2\), \[\begin{align*} \frac{\partial} {\partial\sigma^2} \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) &= -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}} {2(\sigma^2)^2}. \end{align*}\] Setting the derivative equal to zero, \[\begin{align*} -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}} {2(\sigma^2)^2} &= 0 \\ &\implies -n\sigma^2+\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}} = 0 \\ &\implies \sigma^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n}. \end{align*}\] The second derivative is \[ \frac{\partial^2} {\partial(\sigma^2)^2} \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) = \frac{n}{2(\sigma^2)^2} - \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}} {(\sigma^2)^3}. \] At \[ \tilde{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n}, \] we have \[\begin{align*} \left. \frac{\partial^2} {\partial(\sigma^2)^2} \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2\mid\mathbf{y}) \right|_{\sigma^2=\tilde{\sigma}^2} &= -\frac{n}{2(\tilde{\sigma}^2)^2} \\ &< 0. \end{align*}\] Therefore, \[ \tilde{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n} \] maximizes the likelihood. Unlike the regression coefficient estimator, the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is not the same as the unbiased estimator developed previously. This distinction is worth examining. 8.6.3 Maximum Likelihood and Unbiased Estimation of \(\sigma^2\) Recall that the unbiased estimator of the error variance is \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1}. \] The maximum likelihood estimator instead uses the denominator \(n\): \[ \tilde{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n}. \] The difference arises because maximum likelihood and unbiasedness are different estimation criteria. Proposition 8.16 (Bias of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator of the Error Variance) Under the Normal linear regression model with \(p\) explanatory variables and an intercept, \[ \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\sigma}^2] = \frac{n-p-1}{n}\sigma^2. \] Therefore, \[ \operatorname{Bias}(\tilde{\sigma}^2) = -\frac{p+1}{n}\sigma^2, \] and the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is biased downward. Proof Proof. From the previous chapter, \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}] = \sigma^2(n-p-1). \] Therefore, \[\begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\sigma}^2] &= \mathbb{E} \left[ \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n} \right] \\ &= \frac{1}{n} \mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}] \\ &= \frac{n-p-1}{n}\sigma^2. \end{align*}\] Hence, \[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Bias}(\tilde{\sigma}^2) &= \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\sigma}^2]-\sigma^2 \\ &= \frac{n-p-1}{n}\sigma^2-\sigma^2 \\ &= -\frac{p+1}{n}\sigma^2. \end{align*}\] Thus, Maximum Likelihood Estimation and the estimation approach developed in the previous chapter agree for the regression coefficients but not for the error variance: \[ \boxed{ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{MLE} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{OLS}, } \] while \[ \boxed{ \tilde{\sigma}^2_{MLE} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n} \neq \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1} = \hat{\sigma}^2_{\mathrm{unbiased}}. } \] There is no contradiction between these results. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of the observed data, whereas unbiased estimation requires the expectation of an estimator to equal the corresponding parameter. Neither criterion implies the other. The inferential results developed earlier in this chapter used \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1}, \] together with \[ \frac{(n-p-1)\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] Those results therefore remain unchanged by the fact that the maximum likelihood estimator of \(\sigma^2\) uses a different denominator. Maximum Likelihood Estimation gives us another perspective on the role of the Normality assumption. Normality not only provides the exact distributions needed for inference; by specifying the complete distribution of the response, it also allows estimation to be formulated through the likelihood. For the regression coefficients this leads back to the least squares solution, while for the error variance it illustrates that different estimation principles need not produce the same estimator. 8.7 Chapter Synthesis The central purpose of this chapter was to understand what additional information becomes available when the assumptions on the regression errors are strengthened from assumptions about their first two moments to a complete probability distribution. In the previous chapter, the assumptions \[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}]=\mathbf{0} \] and \[ \mathbb{V}[\mathbf{e}]=\sigma^2\mathbf{I} \] were sufficient to establish important properties of the least squares estimators. In particular, they allowed us to study unbiasedness, variances and covariances, the Gauss–Markov result, and unbiased estimation of \(\sigma^2\). The additional assumption introduced in this chapter was \[ \boxed{ \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). } \] This assumption does not change the least squares estimator and is not required for the results established under the weaker mean and variance assumptions. Instead, it provides the additional distributional information needed for exact finite-sample inference. As developed in Section 8.2, Normality implies \[ \mathbf{y} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}). \] Because the least squares estimator, fitted values, and residuals are linear transformations of \(\mathbf{y}\), their complete distributions follow from the moment results obtained previously: \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \right), \] \[ \hat{\mathbf{y}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2\mathbf{H} \right), \] and \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \sim N\left( \mathbf{0}, \sigma^2(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) \right). \] The estimator of the error variance required a different argument because it is based on the quadratic form \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}. \] The geometry developed in the earlier regression chapters becomes especially important here. Since \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}\) is the projection onto the residual subspace and has rank \[ n-p-1, \] Normality implies \[ \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] Equivalently, \[ \frac{(n-p-1)\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-p-1}. \] Thus, the residual degrees of freedom are not merely an algebraic correction in the denominator of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). They correspond to the dimension of the subspace in which the residual vector is allowed to vary. Normality also strengthens the covariance results obtained previously. In particular, \[ \mathbb{C}[\hat{\mathbf{e}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \mathbf{0} \] alone does not imply independence. Under joint Normality, however, \[ \hat{\mathbf{e}} \perp \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \] and consequently \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \perp \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}. \] This independence is one of the key results of the chapter. It allows the Normal distribution of coefficient estimators to be combined with the independent chi-squared distribution used to estimate \(\sigma^2\). The result is the Student’s \(t\) distribution that underlies much of classical regression inference. In Section 8.3, this idea was applied first to a general linear combination \[ \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}. \] The statistic \[ \frac{ \mathbf{a}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta} }{ \hat{\sigma} \sqrt{ \mathbf{a}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{a} } } \] has a Student’s \(t\) distribution with \[ n-p-1 \] degrees of freedom. Individual coefficient intervals and intervals for the expected response are particular cases of this general result. The prediction interval required an additional source of uncertainty. Estimating the mean response at \(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}\) involves uncertainty only through estimation of \[ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}'\boldsymbol{\beta}, \] whereas predicting a future observation also requires accounting for the new error \[ e_{\mathrm{new}}. \] This produces the additional \(1\) in \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 \left[ 1+ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}' (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}} \right]. \] Thus, the distinction between confidence intervals for the mean response and prediction intervals is a direct consequence of the distinction between uncertainty about an unknown mean and randomness in a future observation. The same distributions were used from a different perspective in Section 8.4. A hypothesis test begins by assuming a null hypothesis and determining the distribution of a statistic conditional on that assumption. The \(p\)-value then measures how extreme the observed statistic would be under the distribution implied by the null hypothesis. For regression models, many tests can be understood through comparisons of nested models. If \[ \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_R) \subseteq \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_F), \] then the quantity \[ SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F} \] measures the additional variation explained by enlarging the reduced model to the full model. Under the null hypothesis that the reduced model is sufficient, \[ \frac{ (SS_{res,R}-SS_{res,F})/q }{ SS_{res,F}/\nu } \sim F_{q,\nu}. \] This single construction gives the overall regression test and tests of groups of regression coefficients. The test of an individual coefficient can be viewed in two equivalent ways. The direct approach compares the estimated coefficient with its estimated standard deviation through a \(t\) statistic. The nested-model approach compares the full model with a model in which that explanatory variable has been removed. These two approaches satisfy \[ F_j=T_j^2. \] This equality connects the coefficient-based and geometric interpretations of hypothesis testing. Testing whether \(\beta_j=0\) is equivalent to asking whether the component of \(\mathbf{x}_j\) that cannot already be represented by the remaining explanatory variables produces a sufficiently large reduction in residual variation. Section 8.5 extended the hypothesis-testing framework beyond the null hypothesis. The rejection region of a test is determined using its distribution under \(\mathcal{H}_0\), but power asks for \[ \mathbb{P} \left( \text{reject }\mathcal{H}_0 \mid \text{a specified alternative} \right). \] Under alternatives, the central \(t\) and \(F\) distributions become noncentral distributions. For a single coefficient, the relevant noncentrality parameter is \[ \delta_j = \frac{ \beta_j }{ \sigma \sqrt{ [(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj} } }, \] while for a group of coefficients, \[ \lambda = \frac{ \boldsymbol{\beta}_1' \mathbf{X}_1' (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_2) \mathbf{X}_1 \boldsymbol{\beta}_1 }{ \sigma^2 }. \] These expressions show that power is determined by more than the magnitude of an effect. It also depends on the error variability and on the geometry of the design matrix. The same properties of the explanatory variables that determine the precision of least squares estimation therefore also determine how easily a true effect can be detected. This connection will become particularly important in the Applications chapter, where the direction of the power calculation will be reversed. Rather than treating the design and sample size as fixed and computing power, we will consider how a desired level of power can inform sample-size and study-design decisions. Finally, Section 8.6 used the Normality assumption in a conceptually different way. Once the complete distribution \[ \mathbf{y} \sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}) \] is specified, it becomes possible to construct a likelihood function and estimate the parameters by Maximum Likelihood Estimation. For the regression coefficients, \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{MLE} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{OLS}. \] Thus, least squares and Maximum Likelihood Estimation lead to the same coefficient estimator under the Normal model, even though they begin from different principles. The same agreement does not hold for estimation of \(\sigma^2\): \[ \tilde{\sigma}^2_{MLE} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n}, \] whereas the unbiased estimator used throughout the inferential development is \[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{n-p-1}. \] This distinction emphasizes that maximum likelihood and unbiasedness are different estimation criteria. The fact that the two approaches agree for \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) does not imply that they must agree for every parameter. The conceptual progression of this chapter can therefore be summarized as \[ \boxed{ \begin{array}{c} \mathbf{e}\sim N(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}) \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] \text{Normal distributions for linear transformations} \\[6pt] + \\[6pt] \text{chi-squared distributions for projection-based quadratic forms} \\[6pt] + \\[6pt] \text{independence from joint Normality} \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] t\text{ and }F\text{ distributions} \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] \text{interval estimation and hypothesis testing} \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] \text{noncentral }t\text{ and }F\text{ distributions} \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] \text{power}. \end{array} } \] At the same time, \[ \boxed{ \begin{array}{c} \mathbf{y}\sim N(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{I}) \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] \text{likelihood} \\[6pt] \Downarrow \\[6pt] \text{Maximum Likelihood Estimation}. \end{array} } \] These two branches summarize the main role of the Normality assumption. It converts the moment-based statistical analysis of the previous chapter into a complete finite-sample inferential framework, while also providing a likelihood-based approach to estimation. 8.8 Exercises Let \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}\) be a fixed nonzero vector and consider the hypothesis \[ \mathcal{H}_0: \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}=c \] against \[ \mathcal{H}_1: \mathbf{a}'\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq c, \] where \(c\) is a specified constant. 9 Applications 9.1 ANOVA This section introduces Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) from the viewpoint of the linear regression model. We begin with the simplest case — a single covariate that indicates group membership (one-way ANOVA) — and show how this is equivalent to testing differences in means. We then generalize to the case with additional covariates (ANCOVA), explain how control variables improve estimation, and finish with a discussion of the role of randomization for the covariate of interest. 9.1.1 One-way ANOVA: a single covariate (differences in means) 9.1.1.1 Conceptual statement Suppose we have an outcome \(y\) and a categorical factor with \(G\) groups. Let \(g(i)\in\{1,\dots,G\}\) denote the group of observation \(i\). A one-way ANOVA model can be written as the regression \[ y_i = \mu + \tau_{g(i)} + e_i,\qquad e_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2), \] with the usual constraint \(\sum_{g=1}^G \tau_g = 0\) (identifiability). Equivalently, we can encode the groups with dummy variables and write \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \cdots + \beta_{G-1} x_{G-1,i} + e_i, \] where the \(x_{j,i}\) are indicator (0/1) variables for groups 2..G (group 1 is baseline). Thus one-way ANOVA is an ordinary linear regression in which the covariates are the group indicators. 9.1.1.2 ANOVA as difference-in-means For the two-group case (\(G=2\)) this reduces to testing a difference of means. Let group 1 have mean \(\mu_1\) and group 2 mean \(\mu_2\). The regression \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + e_i, \] with \(x_i=1\) if observation \(i\) is in group 2 and \(0\) otherwise, yields \(\beta_0=\mu_1\) and \(\beta_1=\mu_2-\mu_1\). The hypothesis \[ H_0:\ \mu_1=\mu_2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_0:\ \beta_1=0 \] is then tested by the usual \(t\)-test (or equivalently by an \(F\)-test with 1 numerator df). The one-way ANOVA \(F\) statistic for general \(G\) compares between-group variability to within-group variability; algebraically it is the same as the regression \(F\) that compares the model with group indicators to the intercept-only model. 9.1.1.3 R example — one-way ANOVA / difference in means # Example: the built-in 'sleep' dataset (two groups). data(sleep) # R's sleep dataset: extra sleep for two groups head(sleep) ## extra group ID ## 1 0.7 1 1 ## 2 -1.6 1 2 ## 3 -0.2 1 3 ## 4 -1.2 1 4 ## 5 -0.1 1 5 ## 6 3.4 1 6 # Fit one-way ANOVA using aov (equivalent to lm with factor) fit_aov <- aov(extra ~ group, data = sleep) summary(fit_aov) ## Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) ## group 1 12.48 12.482 3.463 0.0792 . ## Residuals 18 64.89 3.605 ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 # Fit the equivalent linear model with a dummy fit_lm <- lm(extra ~ factor(group), data = sleep) summary(fit_lm) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = extra ~ factor(group), data = sleep) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -2.430 -1.305 -0.580 1.455 3.170 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) 0.7500 0.6004 1.249 0.2276 ## factor(group)2 1.5800 0.8491 1.861 0.0792 . ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 1.899 on 18 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.1613, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1147 ## F-statistic: 3.463 on 1 and 18 DF, p-value: 0.07919 Explanation of the code We use the built-in sleep dataset, which contains the sleep extra hours in two groups. aov(extra ~ group, data = sleep) fits the one-way ANOVA model. lm(extra ~ factor(group), ...) fits the equivalent regression with group indicators; summary reports coefficients and tests. The F test in aov and the \(t\) test for the group coefficient in lm are numerically equivalent for the two-group problem. 9.2 ANCOVA 9.2.0.1 Concept and notation When additional continuous covariates are present, we may want to test group differences after controlling for these covariates. This is the Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) framework. Suppose \(\mathbf{z}_i\) is a vector of control variables for observation \(i\). The ANCOVA model is: \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_{\text{grp}}' \mathbf{x}_{i} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}'\mathbf{z}_i + e_i, \] where \(\mathbf{x}_i\) are group indicator variables and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) are coefficients for the controls. The hypothesis that the \(k\) group effects are zero (no group differences after adjustment) is \[ H_0:\ \beta_{\text{grp}} = \mathbf{0}. \] 9.2.1 How controls act as “partialling out” Adding \(\mathbf{z}\) does two things: Reduces omitted-variable bias (if \(\mathbf{z}\) is confounded with group): by adjusting for covariates associated with both group and outcome, we make the conditional interpretation of \(\beta_{\text{grp}}\) closer to a causal or conditional effect. Improves precision: if \(\mathbf{z}\) explains variance in \(y\), then residual variance \(\sigma^2\) is smaller, which reduces the variance of coefficient estimators and increases power to detect group effects. In matrix terms, let \(\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{X}*{\text{grp}},\mathbf{Z}]\) be the full design matrix (group indicators and controls). The variance of the estimated group coefficients depends on the block \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\). If \(\mathbf{Z}\) explains variation in \(y\) but is not collinear with \(\mathbf{X}*{\text{grp}}\), the diagonal entries of \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) relevant to group coefficients shrink, improving standard errors. 9.2.2 Partial F-test in ANCOVA To test group effects controlling for \(\mathbf{z}\), compare: Reduced model (controls only): \(y \sim \mathbf{Z}\), SSR\(_{\text{red}}\). Full model (controls + groups): \(y \sim \mathbf{Z} + \mathbf{X}*{\text{grp}}\), SSR\(*{\text{full}}\). The partial F statistic is \[ F = \frac{(\text{SSR}*{\text{red}}-\text{SSR}*{\text{full}})/k}{\text{SSR}*{\text{full}}/(n-p*{\text{full}})}, \] with \(k\) = number of group d.f. in numerator. Under \(H_0\) this follows \(F_{k, n-p_{\text{full}}}\). 9.2.3 R example — ANCOVA with mtcars We analyze whether the number of cylinders (cyl) affects mpg after controlling for weight (wt) and horsepower (hp). data(mtcars) # Fit reduced model: controls only fit_red <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars) # Fit full model: controls + group indicator (cyl as factor) fit_full <- lm(mpg ~ factor(cyl) + wt + hp, data = mtcars) # Partial F-test anova(fit_red, fit_full) ## Analysis of Variance Table ## ## Model 1: mpg ~ wt + hp ## Model 2: mpg ~ factor(cyl) + wt + hp ## Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) ## 1 29 195.05 ## 2 27 160.78 2 34.27 2.8776 0.07364 . ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 # Summaries summary(fit_full) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = mpg ~ factor(cyl) + wt + hp, data = mtcars) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -4.2612 -1.0320 -0.3210 0.9281 5.3947 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Reduction in residual variance. If the controls explain genuine variation in \(y\), then \(\hat\sigma^2\) from the full model is smaller than from a model without controls. Since standard errors for coefficients are proportional to \(\hat\sigma\), this increases power. Removal of confounding. If group membership is correlated with control covariates that also affect \(y\), failing to control will bias the estimated group differences. Conditioning on \(\mathbf{Z}\) recovers the conditional association of groups with \(y\). Interpretation: conditional effects. Coefficients of the group indicators in the ANCOVA are interpreted as mean differences conditional on the controls. Caveat — multicollinearity. If some controls are highly collinear with group indicators (e.g., almost all observations in one group have similar control values), then \((\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) inflates and standard errors can increase. Design and variable selection matter. 9.3 Effect of randomization in the covariate of interest Randomization of the treatment (or group assignment) is central to causal inference and also simplifies the ANOVA/ANCOVA analysis. 9.3.1 Key consequences of randomization Balance (in expectation). With random assignment, treatment groups are, in expectation, balanced on both observed and unobserved covariates: \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Z}\mid \text{treatment}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Z}]\). As a result, simple between-group comparisons are unbiased for the average treatment effect without needing adjustment for covariates. Orthogonality. Under complete randomization, the group indicators are (approximately) orthogonal to pre-treatment covariates; formally, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_{\text{grp}},\mathbf{Z})\approx \mathbf{0}\) in large samples. This orthogonality yields simpler variance expressions and better behaved estimates. Precision gain from adjusting. Even with randomization, adjusting for prognostic covariates in ANCOVA can increase precision (reduce standard errors) because controls explain residual variance. Because orthogonality prevents bias in coefficient estimates, adjustment is safe and typically recommended. Finite-sample exactness. In randomized experiments with certain designs (e.g., completely randomized with normal errors), tests based on regression or ANOVA can be made exact (valid in finite samples), not only asymptotically. 9.3.2 Randomized vs observational assignments Randomized assignment: identification of the causal effect is straightforward; regression adjustments mainly improve precision. Observational assignment: group differences may reflect confounding; adjustments are necessary to reduce bias, but residual confounding can remain. 9.3.3 Simulation example: randomized vs non-randomized (brief) set.seed(123) n <- 200 # Covariate strongly predictive of y z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Scenario A: randomized treatment t_rand <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5) # random 0/1 assignment y_rand <- 1.5 * t_rand + 2 * z + rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Scenario B: observational treatment correlated with z p_obs <- plogis(0.5 * z) # higher z -> more likely treated t_obs <- rbinom(n, 1, p_obs) y_obs <- 1.5 * t_obs + 2 * z + rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Estimate treatment effect without and with control summary(lm(y_rand ~ t_rand)) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = y_rand ~ t_rand) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -6.1757 -1.5970 -0.2269 1.5051 5.9601 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. In the randomized scenario (t_rand) treatment is independent of z. The unadjusted regression y ~ t_rand gives an (approximately) unbiased estimate of the treatment effect; adding z reduces the standard error. In the observational scenario, treatment depends on z (t_obs), creating confounding. The unadjusted regression y ~ t_obs is biased; adding z recovers a more accurate estimate (and reduces bias), though perfect adjustment requires all confounders to be observed. 9.3.4 Practical guidance and summary ANOVA = Regression. One-way ANOVA is a linear regression with group indicator covariates. Testing for equal means is testing coefficients of those indicators. ANCOVA = ANOVA + controls. Adding covariates adjusts for confounding and improves precision when covariates explain outcome variability. Partial F-tests compare nested models (with and without group indicators) controlling for other covariates; algebraically these are the same sums-of-squares comparisons used in classical ANOVA. Randomization guarantees unbiasedness of group comparisons and typically simplifies inference; even when randomized, adjustment for prognostic covariates is advisable to gain efficiency. Check assumptions. Classical ANOVA/ANCOVA relies on linearity, homoscedasticity (or robust alternatives), and (for exact small-sample \(p\)-values) normality of errors; diagnostics remain important. 9.3.5 ANOVA sums-of-squares as projection (matrix) decomposition Below is a concise derivation that shows how the classical ANOVA decomposition of sums of squares maps directly to the regression decomposition using projection (hat) matrices. The derivation assumes the model includes an intercept (so that the column space of the intercept is the space of constant vectors). 9.3.5.1 Notation \(\mathbf{y}\): \(n\times 1\) response vector. \(\mathbf{X}\): \(n\times p\) design matrix including a column of ones for the intercept. \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\): hat (projection) matrix onto \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\). \(\mathbf{H}_0 = \dfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\): hat matrix for the intercept-only model (projection onto constant vectors). \(\mathbf{I}\): \(n\times n\) identity matrix. All projection matrices above are symmetric and idempotent. 9.3.5.2 Total Sum of Squares (SST) Classically, the total sum of squares (using the mean as baseline) is \[ \text{SST}=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar{y})^2. \] In matrix form this is \[ \text{SST} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}, \] because \(\mathbf{H}_0\mathbf{y}=\bar{y}\,\mathbf{1}\) is the projection of \(\mathbf{y}\) onto the constant vector. 9.3.5.3 Error (Residual) Sum of Squares (SSE) The residual sum of squares from the full model is \[ \text{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}, \] since \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is the projection of \(\mathbf{y}\) onto \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\). 9.3.5.4 Regression (Between) Sum of Squares (SSR) The regression (or explained) sum of squares is defined by the identity \[ \text{SSR} = \text{SST} - \text{SSE}. \] Using the matrix forms above, \[\begin{align*} \text{SSR} &= \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y} \\ &= \mathbf{y}'\big(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0\big)\mathbf{y}. \end{align*}\] Thus the portion of variability explained by the full model (over and above the intercept-only model) is the quadratic form with the idempotent matrix \(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0\), which projects onto the subspace of \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{X})\) orthogonal to the constant vector. 9.3.5.5 Orthogonality and additivity Because \(\mathbf{H}\) and \(\mathbf{H}_0\) are projection matrices with \(\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{H}_0)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(\mathbf{H})\), the difference \[ \mathbf{M} \;=\; \mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0 \] is itself symmetric and idempotent, and projects onto the \(p-1\) dimensional subspace of predictors after removing the intercept. One checks that \[ (\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{0}, \] so the subspace onto which \(\mathbf{M}\) projects is orthogonal to the residual space of the full model. From this orthogonality it follows immediately that \[ \text{SST} = \text{SSR} + \text{SSE}, \] i.e. the sums-of-squares add (because the corresponding quadratic forms are on orthogonal subspaces). 9.3.5.6 Degrees of freedom and trace The degrees of freedom associated to each sum of squares are equal to the trace (rank) of the corresponding idempotent matrix: \(\text{df}_{\text{Total}} = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0) = n-1\). \(\text{df}_{\text{Regression}} = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H})-\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}_0) = p - 1\). \(\text{df}_{\text{Error}} = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) = n - p\). These trace identities give the familiar ANOVA degrees-of-freedom breakdown. 9.3.5.7 Remarks The matrix viewpoint makes transparent that one-way ANOVA, multiple regression, and ANCOVA are the same algebraic object: sums of squares are quadratic forms induced by projections onto nested linear subspaces. The decomposition and orthogonality arguments above are the backbone of ANOVA inference and of the construction of \(F\)-tests: a difference of quadratic forms projecting onto an added subspace yields a (scaled) \(\chi^2\) in the numerator, independent of the residual \(\chi^2\) in the denominator, producing the \(F\)-statistic. 9.4 Variance decomposition 9.4.1 Notation (common to both derivations) There are \(k\) groups. Group \(j\) has \(n_j\) observations, \(j=1,\dots,k\), and total sample size \(n=\sum_{j=1}^k n_j\). Let \(y_{j i}\) be the \(i\)th observation in group \(j\) (\(i=1,\dots,n_j\)). Group means: \(\bar y_{j\cdot}=\dfrac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} y_{j i}\). Overall (grand) mean: \(\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} y_{j i}\). We define the standard sums of squares: Total sum of squares (SST) \[ \mathrm{SST}=\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2. \] Within-groups (error) sum of squares (SSE) \[ \mathrm{SSE}=\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i}-\bar y_{j\cdot})^2. \] Between-groups (regression/explained) sum of squares (SSB) \[ \mathrm{SSB}=\sum_{j=1}^k n_j(\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2. \] The ANOVA identity to prove is \[ \mathrm{SST}=\mathrm{SSB}+\mathrm{SSE}. \] 9.4.2 1 — Scalar (elementwise) derivation Start from the decomposition of each deviation from the grand mean as the sum of a within-group deviation and the group mean deviation: \[ y_{j i} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot} = (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot}) + (\bar y_{j\cdot} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot}). \] Square both sides and sum over all observations: \[\begin{align*} \mathrm{SST} &= \sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2 \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} \big[ (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot}) + (\bar y_{j\cdot} - \bar y_{\cdot\cdot}) \big]^2 \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot})^2 + 2\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot})(\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}) + \sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2 \end{align*}\] Now simplify the middle term. For a fixed group \(j\), \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot}) = 0 \] by the definition of the group mean. Therefore the cross term vanishes: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot})(\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}) = (\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(y_{j i}-\bar y_{j\cdot}) = 0. \] Hence the expansion reduces to \[ \mathrm{SST} = \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} (y_{j i} - \bar y_{j\cdot})^2}_{\mathrm{SSE}} + \underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^k n_j(\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2}_{\mathrm{SSB}}. \] That is, \[ \boxed{\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSB} + \mathrm{SSE}.} \] This is the usual elementary proof used in introductory courses. 9.4.3 2 — Matrix / projection derivation The matrix derivation exposes the geometric reason: ANOVA is a decomposition of the data vector \(\mathbf{y}\) into orthogonal projections. Form the \(n\times 1\) stacked data vector \(\mathbf{y}\) (stack all observations in any order). Let \(\mathbf{1}\) be the \(n\times 1\) vector of ones, \(\mathbf{H}_0=\dfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\) be the projection onto the constant (intercept) subspace, \(\mathbf{X}\) be the \(n\times k\) design matrix of group indicators in cell-means or contrast form (a column for each group mean or \(k-1\) columns plus an intercept — the projection subspace is the same), \(\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\) be the hat matrix projecting onto the group subspace (all vectors constant within groups). Then SST, SSE and SSB can be written as quadratic forms: Total: \[ \mathrm{SST} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}. \] (This measures deviation from the grand mean.) Error (within groups): \[ \mathrm{SSE} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}. \] Between groups: \[ \mathrm{SSB} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}. \] These identities are immediate from the definitions of the projection matrices (e.g. \(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}=\widehat{\mathbf{y}}\) is the vector of fitted values, constant within each group). Now note that (algebraically) \[ \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0 = (\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0) + (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}). \] Indeed rearrange: \[ (\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0) + (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}) = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H}_0. \] Thus the three quadratic forms add: \[ \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}, \] which is \[ \mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSB} + \mathrm{SSE}. \] Geometrically, \(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0\) and \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}\) are orthogonal projectors: they project onto orthogonal subspaces (the explained subspace orthogonal to the intercept, and the residual subspace), so their quadratic forms are additive. The ranks (traces) of these idempotent matrices give the usual degrees of freedom: \[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{df}(\mathrm{SST}) &= n-1,\ \mathrm{df}(\mathrm{SSB}) &= k-1,\ \mathrm{df}(\mathrm{SSE}) &= n-k, \end{aligned}\] () &= k-1, () &= n-k, \end{aligned} and the additivity of degrees of freedom follows from the trace additivity of the matrices. 9.4.4 Concluding remarks The elementary expansion shows the identity by direct algebra and uses only the fact that group deviations sum to zero. The matrix proof reveals the deeper geometric reason: ANOVA decomposes \(\mathbf{y}\) into orthogonal projection components (grand-mean, group effects, residual), and orthogonality implies additivity of sums of squares. Either viewpoint is useful: the scalar proof is easy and constructive; the matrix viewpoint generalizes directly to ANCOVA, factorial ANOVA, and the projection-based distributional results (chi-square / \(F\) tests).
